Living with patience and non-reactivity is not just for the future; it instantly improves our physical health, reduces stress, preserves our relationships, and fills our present life with genuine joy and dignity. --- CHAPTER 7

text_modern: Now that you have cultivated patience, you must develop persistent energy, for awakening itself is rooted in energy. Without energy, spiritual growth is impossible, just as there is no movement without the wind.

translator_notes: In Buddhist psychology, energy (virya) is the enthusiastic effort directed toward the wholesome. Just as patience prevents us from reacting destructively, energy provides the active force needed for positive transformation and awakening (bodhi).

text_modern: What is energy? It is the courage to do good. Its enemies are laziness, attachment to harmful habits, discouragement, and self-contempt.

translator_notes: Self-contempt (or self-deprecation) is recognized here as a major psychological barrier to personal growth. Believing that we are incapable of change or too flawed to achieve peace is a form of cognitive distortion that drains our energy.

text_modern: Inertia, craving for worldly pleasures, mental dullness, and a dependency on external comfort make us blind to the suffering of existence. This is how laziness is born.

translator_notes: Psychological comfort zones and fleeting pleasures often desensitize us to the underlying anxieties of life (samsara), leading to spiritual and emotional stagnation.

text_modern: You are at the mercy of those hunters—your own destructive passions—having fallen into the net of conditioned existence. How can you not yet see that you have walked straight into the jaws of death?

translator_notes: Passions (kleshas) act like internal captors that trap us in cycles of suffering. Realizing our mortality and the impermanence of things serves as a powerful therapeutic wake-up call to break free from these habitual patterns.

text_modern: Can you not see your fellow beings dying one after another? And yet, you still surrender to laziness, like an ox waiting passively in the slaughterhouse.

translator_notes: Denying death is a common defense mechanism. Confronting the reality of impermanence shakes us out of our psychological sleepwalk.

text_modern: Death is watching you; every escape route is closed. How can you find careless pleasure in food, sleep, or romance?

translator_notes: "Yama" in the French text is the personification of death and time. The text urges us not to seek temporary distractions or escape into sensory pleasures when the fundamental challenges of existence remain unaddressed.

text_modern: When death finishes its preparations and strikes, you will suddenly want to shake off your laziness, but it will be too late. What will you do then?

translator_notes: Procrastination is a form of emotional avoidance. The author warns of the deep regret and panic that arise when we realize we have wasted our time on trivialities. Clean_Text: "This is still left to do... this is only just begun... this is only half-finished... and now, death is suddenly here!" This is what you will think as you look upon your heartbroken family, their eyes red and swollen with tears, while facing the terrifying messengers of death. Context_Notes: This captures the psychological distress of incomplete life tasks and the realization of unfulfilled potential at the moment of death. It encourages living mindfully and intentionally in the present.

text_modern: Tortured by the memory of your past misdeeds, hearing the cries of torment, lost in panic and soiled by your own terror—what will you do in that moment of absolute helplessness?

translator_notes: The psychological hell described here is the acute guilt, shame, and terror of facing the consequences of one's unskilful actions without mental preparation.

text_modern: "I am like a fish caught in a net." This is the realization that should shake you in this very life, knowing the deep, self-created suffering that awaits an unawakened mind.

translator_notes: Recognizing the trap of our habitual conditioning is the first step toward seeking liberation. The "fish in the net" is a metaphor for being trapped by our own unconscious impulses.

text_modern: You are so delicate that you cry out when touched by warm water. How, then, can you remain so complacent while carrying the heavy burden of actions that lead to immense psychological torment?

translator_notes: This highlights the contradiction between our physical hypersensitivity and our spiritual carelessness, urging us to take mental hygiene seriously.

text_modern: You are lazy yet you crave rewards; you are fragile yet you invite suffering; you are already in the grip of death yet you behave as if you are immortal. Oh, foolish one, you are driving yourself to ruin!

translator_notes: This addresses cognitive dissonance: wanting positive psychological outcomes (peace, happiness) while repeatedly engaging in negative habits (laziness, avoidance) and pretending death won't happen to us.

text_modern: You possess this precious vessel of human life—use it to cross the great river of suffering! Foolish one, this is no time to sleep, for such an opportunity is extremely rare to find again.

translator_notes: Human life is viewed as a unique psychological and spiritual vehicle (the ship) equipped with self-awareness and the capacity to transcend suffering. Wasting it is a profound loss.

text_modern: How can you reject the sublime joy of meaningful purpose—the source of endless peace—only to chase after superficial distractions and empty laughter that lead only to pain?

translator_notes: Distinguishing between eudaimonic happiness (meaningful, virtuous living) and hedonic pleasure (fleeting, distractive sensory gratification). True, lasting joy comes from spiritual practice and serving others.

text_modern: Courage, focused inner strength, constant diligence, self-control, identifying yourself with others, and exchanging yourself for others—these are the key components of energy.

translator_notes: Energy is not just physical stamina but a psychological composite of determination, mindfulness, and empathy. Crucially, compassion for others is a primary source of this transformative drive. Clean_Text: Do not lose heart, thinking, "How could I ever achieve awakening?" For the truthful Buddha has spoken this ultimate truth: even those who were once gnats, mosquitoes, flies, and worms have, through their persistent efforts, attained the supreme state of awakening. Context_Notes: An antidote to low self-esteem and helplessness. If even the simplest creatures can eventually evolve and achieve peace, a human being endowed with reason and self-awareness certainly can.

text_modern: Since I have been born a human being, with the capacity to distinguish between what heals and what harms, why should I not achieve awakening if I simply follow the paths shown by the wise?

translator_notes: Emphasizes our innate agency and capacity for rational discernment. We have the psychological tools necessary for self-realization; we only need to apply them.

text_modern: Yet I find myself trembling at the thought of sacrificing my hands, my feet, or my limbs. This fear arises because, in my confusion, I mistake what is trivial for what is truly profound.

translator_notes: Fear of sacrifice is a common psychological defense. The text prepares us for gradual growth, pointing out that our current anxiety about letting go of our physical attachment is based on a narrow perspective of self-preservation. Clean_Text: What is truly terrifying is the endless, self-inflicted pain of staying trapped in suffering for ages without ever finding freedom. The small discomfort of spiritual discipline is insignificant; it is like the brief pain of pulling out a deeply embedded thorn, which finally puts an end to your suffering. Context_Notes: This uses a powerful therapeutic analogy: facing the pain of growth is like undergoing a necessary medical procedure. The temporary discomfort of therapy or discipline is minor compared to the chronic, lifetime pain of remaining unhealed.

text_modern: All healers cure diseases through procedures that cause temporary discomfort. Therefore, we must endure a little discomfort to eliminate profound suffering.

translator_notes: Healing is rarely pain-free. Confronting our shadow, breaking toxic habits, and practicing discipline involve emotional discomfort, but they are necessary steps toward long-term mental well-being.

text_modern: Yet, even though the cure is beneficial, the wise physician does not demand difficult treatments from a beginner. He starts with gentle remedies to heal severe illnesses.

translator_notes: A compassionate approach to self-improvement. Just like in psychotherapy, changes must be introduced gradually so as not to overwhelm the individual, respecting their current window of tolerance.

text_modern: At first, the Guide instructs his disciple to practice giving simple things, like vegetables or food. Only gradually, step by step, does he guide them to the point where they can effortlessly sacrifice their own comfort and body.

translator_notes: Systematic desensitization and gradual training. We build our psychological capacity for generosity and selflessness by starting with small, risk-free actions.

text_modern: When one develops the inner realization that sees their own body as no different from simple food, they feel no pain or hesitation in giving up everything they have.

translator_notes: De-centering from the physical ego. Once the deep identification with the physical body is softened, the fear of loss vanishes, leading to ultimate psychological freedom.

text_modern: Purified of harmful habits, one is protected from physical suffering; wise, they are free from mental anguish. For the mind suffers because of cognitive errors, and the body suffers from unwholesome actions.

translator_notes: Demonstrates the mind-body connection in suffering. Mental distress is caused by delusion (cognitive distortions), while physical distress is often the natural result of reckless and harmful behaviors.

text_modern: The body is sustained by virtue, and the heart is made joyful by wisdom. Since such a person chooses to remain in this world solely out of compassion to help others, what could possibly make them suffer?

translator_notes: For an awakened being (bodhisattva), living in the world is not a burden but an act of love. Their virtue and wisdom act as a psychological shield, transforming potential suffering into purposeful service.

text_modern: By dissolving past negative conditioning and accumulating vast oceans of positive mental energy, they progress toward liberation far more swiftly than those who seek peace only for themselves.

translator_notes: Altruistic motivation (the Bodhisattva path) is psychologically more powerful and accelerating than individualistic motivation (the Hearer/Auditeur path, Note 47). Compassion expands our capacity and speed for healing.

text_modern: Moving thus from joy to joy, what sensible person could ever become discouraged when they ride upon the vehicle of the spirit of awakening—a path that frees them from all inner pain and exhaustion?

translator_notes: Altruistic action is inherently self-sustaining and energizing. When our life's purpose is aligned with the well-being of others, we find a deep, exhaustless source of psychological energy and joy.

text_modern: To achieve the liberation of all beings, you must mobilize an army of four strengths: deep aspiration, healthy self-confidence, joyful enthusiasm, and the wisdom of letting go.

translator_notes: Louis Finot translates these four as "Aspiration" (chanda), "Fierté" (mana - used here in the positive sense of self-respect or divine confidence), "Joie" (rati), and "Renonciation" (mukti - letting go or resting in freedom). Together, they form the psychological framework for sustained positive action.

text_modern: Deep aspiration is developed by reflecting on the terrifying reality of suffering and realizing the profound benefits of the path.

translator_notes: Aspiration is fueled by both "away-from" motivation (understanding the pain of remaining unhealed) and "toward" motivation (realizing the peace and joy of emotional freedom). This corresponds to Finot's introductory line to the "Aspiration" section.

text_modern: I have countless destructive habits to dissolve, both within myself and for the sake of others. In this monumental task, clearing away even a single pattern of harm can take vast lifetimes of effort.

translator_notes: This verse acknowledges the sheer scale of psychological shadow-work. Undoing deeply ingrained trauma and unconscious conditioning is a long-term process that requires immense patience and persistence (Note 49).

text_modern: Yet for this great work of transforming my mind, I see within myself barely a spark of energy. Knowing that I am heading toward endless self-created suffering, how is it that my heart does not break with urgency?

translator_notes: A cry of existential urgency. It highlights the pain of realizing one's own apathy and the discrepancy between the magnitude of our psychological challenges and our actual efforts.

text_modern: I must cultivate countless positive qualities, for my own healing and for others. Yet, the deep integration of even a single virtue takes ages to truly master.

translator_notes: Building healthy psychological traits (virtues) is just as slow and deliberate as removing negative habits. It requires continuous, conscious practice over time.

text_modern: And yet, I have not truly mastered even a small fraction of these qualities. I have wasted this extraordinary human life, which is so incredibly rare and difficult to obtain.

translator_notes: Confronting the regret of squandered opportunities. Cultivating self-awareness allows us to appreciate the preciousness of our current mental and physical capacity before it is lost.

text_modern: I have not known the joy of celebrating the awakened ones; I have not honored the path of truth, nor have I fulfilled the hopes of those in need.

translator_notes: Experiencing regret for past self-centeredness and lack of service. Giving to others and honoring wisdom are deep sources of psychological nourishment that we often neglect.

text_modern: I have not brought safety to those in danger, nor have I comforted those who suffer. I have been nothing but a source of pain and anxiety to the mother who bore me.

translator_notes: A candid self-reflection on the pain we inflict on our loved ones when we live unconsciously. Recognizing this is a painful but necessary step in relational healing.

text_modern: It is because I lacked aspiration for the truth in the past that I find myself in such mental confusion today. Knowing this, who would ever want to abandon their pursuit of the truth now?

translator_notes: Our current mental state is the result of past habits. Understanding this causal relationship (karma) motivates us to change our present actions to shape a healthier future.

text_modern: The Buddha declared that aspiration is the root of all positive transformation, and this aspiration is nurtured by deeply reflecting on the natural consequences of our actions.

translator_notes: Intention and aspiration are the starting points of behavioral change. By visualizing and contemplating the positive outcomes of wholesome actions and the painful results of harmful ones, we build intrinsic motivation.

text_modern: Physical pain, mental anguish, constant dangers, and the ultimate shattering of all their desires—this is the natural harvest of those who continue to sow seeds of harm.

translator_notes: A psychological description of the feedback loop of negative behavior. Living destructively naturally results in anxiety, broken relationships, and internal chaos.

text_modern: But the desires of those who act with kindness and wisdom will, through the power of their positive actions, find fulfillment and peace, welcomed like long-awaited guests.

translator_notes: Living in alignment with values and virtues builds a harmonious mind, which naturally attracts positive life outcomes and emotional resilience.

text_modern: Conversely, the desperate search for happiness by those who act out of selfishness and hatred will always be cut short by the sharp blades of self-created pain.

translator_notes: This highlights the paradox of hedonism and selfish pursuit: trying to grasp happiness through harmful means inevitably destroys the very peace we seek.

text_modern: Nurtured within the cool, fragrant petals of massive lotus flowers, their radiant minds fed by the gentle, wise words of the Awakened One, those who act with love emerge beautifully into the light of ultimate wisdom.

translator_notes: A poetic depiction of the psychological rebirth into a state of pure compassion and clarity, symbolized by emerging from a lotus in the pure land of Amitabha (Sukhāvatī, Note 50).

text_modern: Meanwhile, those who live in hatred find themselves screaming in a hell of their own making, their minds scorched by burning guilt, their emotions torn to shreds by sharp regrets, falling repeatedly into states of intense self-torment.

translator_notes: This translates the physical imagery of hell into the psychological reality of acute remorse, self-hatred, and mental torment that follow destructive behaviors.

text_modern: Therefore, let us eagerly cultivate our aspiration for the good. Having nurtured it deeply, we must then build a sacred self-confidence, following the teachings of the scriptures.

translator_notes: "Fierté" (pride) is used here as a translation for positive self-confidence, self-efficacy, or healthy self-concept. It is the bold conviction that "I can and will overcome these obstacles," which is vital for therapeutic change. Reference is made to the Vajradhvaja-sutra.

text_modern: First, honestly assess your inner strength before taking on a commitment. It is far better to wait and prepare than to begin and abandon the work halfway.

translator_notes: Encourages realistic goal-setting and self-evaluation. Embarking on deep psychological work or life commitments without assessing one's current capacity can lead to a sense of failure and learned helplessness.

text_modern: For if you abandon your commitments, the habit of giving up will carry over, compounding your self-doubt, wasting your precious time, and leaving you with nothing but half-finished efforts.

translator_notes: The psychological pattern of repeatedly quitting reinforces a negative self-concept of failure. Sticking to manageable commitments builds self-trust and resilience.

text_modern: This sacred confidence applies to three areas: your actions, your struggle against destructive emotions, and your spiritual capacity. The confidence of action is saying: "I will carry out this work myself!"

translator_notes: Developing agency and taking full responsibility for one's life. Instead of waiting for external rescue, the individual resolves to actively participate in their own healing and service.

text_modern: Trapped by their own painful habits, the people of this world are often unable to free themselves. Therefore, I must take up this work for them, for I am not powerless to change.

translator_notes: Empathy and responsibility. Seeing others struggle with mental illness or toxic emotions should not make us judgmental, but rather inspire us to act as steady, healthy anchors for them.

text_modern: Why should anyone else have to do the difficult and humbling work when I am right here to help? If selfish pride stops me from serving, then let my pride be utterly destroyed!

translator_notes: An antidote to entitlement and elitism. True self-confidence is humble and willing to perform any service, whereas insecure ego-pride avoids "lowly" tasks out of fear of looking bad.

text_modern: Even a crow behaves like a giant eagle when it finds a tiny dead lizard. In the same way, if my mind is weak, even the smallest temptation will easily overpower me.

translator_notes: A vivid metaphor for psychological fragility. When we lack inner strength and mindfulness, even trivial distractions or minor irritations can dominate our emotional state.

text_modern: When you surrender to discouragement and inaction, you easily fall prey to negative habits. But when you are alert and enthusiastic, you can stand firm against the most powerful internal demons.

translator_notes: Behavioral activation. Staying active and engaged protects us from the depressive spiral of self-doubt and lethargy.

text_modern: Therefore, with a steadfast heart, I will conquer my own downfalls. How absurd it is to dream of changing the world if I cannot even master my own impulses!

translator_notes: Self-mastery must precede social transformation. We cannot hope to bring peace to others if we are constantly ruled by our own dysregulated emotions.

text_modern: I must conquer all my inner obstacles and refuse to let anything conquer me. This is the noble self-respect I must awaken, for I am a child of the courageous, awakened teachers!

translator_notes: Finding strength in spiritual lineage and innate potential. This is a therapeutic affirmation of worth, reminding ourselves that we are capable of overcoming any mental adversity.

text_modern: Those who are ruled by toxic pride are actually insecure and fragile, not strong. For a truly proud person would never surrender to an enemy, yet these people willingly submit to their greatest enemy: their own ego.

translator_notes: Distinguishing between toxic, defensive pride (which is born of insecurity and keeps us stuck in egoic habits) and healthy self-respect (which refuses to be enslaved by negative emotions). Clean_Text: Toxic pride only drags them down into misery. Even in this life, they live without genuine joy, constantly dependent on others, feeling inadequate, isolated, and paralyzed by their own arrogance. If such miserable souls are called "proud," then tell me, who is truly degraded? Context_Notes: Arrogance often acts as a mask for deep-seated feelings of worthlessness and dependency. It isolates people, making them emotionally impoverished and miserable.

text_modern: The true heroes are those who direct their pride toward defeating the ego itself. Having conquered this trembling enemy, they can freely share the sweet fruits of their emotional victory with the entire world.

translator_notes: Turning self-assertive energy inward. Instead of using our will to dominate others, we use it to conquer our own self-centered arrogance, which then allows us to be of genuine help to the world (Note 51).

text_modern: Even when surrounded by a swarm of destructive emotions, stand a thousand times firmer, remaining completely untouched by them, just as a lion stands fearless among a herd of deer.

translator_notes: Cultivating emotional sovereignty. Mindfulness and self-respect allow us to remain centered and unswayed, even when surrounded by chaotic, negative environments or internal triggers.

text_modern: Just as no amount of urgency can make your eyes taste flavor, no amount of hardship should ever force an awakening heart to surrender to toxic, destructive passions.

translator_notes: Unshakable boundary of integrity. Just as physical organs have natural limits, a well-trained mind establishes clear, unbreakable boundaries against slipping into harmful reactive behaviors.

text_modern: You must immerse yourself in the work you undertake with passion and delight, with an insatiable heart, like a player completely captivated by the joy of the game.

translator_notes: Entering the state of "flow." Healthy action is not a chore but an engaging, joyful play. When we find deep purpose in helping others, we act with enthusiastic, playful energy.

text_modern: While people act in hopes of finding future happiness—which may or may not come—the person whose happiness lies in the act of helping itself finds joy in every moment. How could they ever be happy standing idle?

translator_notes: This captures the essence of intrinsic motivation. If your joy is in the process of compassionate action rather than grasping for external results, your happiness is secure and independent of circumstances.

text_modern: If we never grow tired of chasing worldly pleasures—which are like licking sweet honey from a sharp razor blade—how could we ever tire of tasting the nectar of wholesome actions, which bring nothing but deep peace and healing?

translator_notes: Chasing fleeting sensory pleasures is inherently risky and never truly satisfying (like licking honey off a razor). In contrast, cultivating virtues and helping others yields a safe, enriching, and deeply satisfying mental state.

text_modern: Therefore, as soon as one meaningful task is complete, immerse yourself in the next, just as an elephant, scorched by the midday sun, plunges eagerly into the cool waters of a lake.

translator_notes: Reconditioning our sources of reward. Instead of seeking rest in passive distraction, a healthy mind finds its rejuvenation and rest in continuous, meaningful engagement.

text_modern: If your energy is completely spent, rest and recharge for a while. And when a task is successfully completed, set it down gently, ready and eager for the next step of the journey.

translator_notes: Compassionate self-care. It is vital to recognize our physical and emotional limits to avoid burnout. Resting is not laziness; it is a necessary part of sustaining long-term, positive effort.

text_modern: Stay highly vigilant against the sudden attacks of your toxic emotions, parrying them swiftly, like a skilled warrior engaged in an intense duel.

translator_notes: Active coping. Mental habits do not disappear passively; we must actively catch and redirect negative thoughts as soon as they arise, especially when triggered.

text_modern: In the heat of battle, if a warrior drops their sword, they quickly pick it up in fear. In the same way, if you lose your sword of mindfulness, retrieve it immediately, knowing the mental chaos that awaits without it.

translator_notes: Recovery of mindfulness. It is natural to lose focus or fall back into old triggers occasionally. The key is not to judge ourselves, but to immediately restore our awareness (mindfulness) before negative thoughts take over.

text_modern: Just as poison entering the bloodstream quickly spreads throughout the body, a single negative habit, if allowed to find a crack in your awareness, will rapidly flood your entire mind.

translator_notes: Emotional contagion within the self. A small moment of unchecked resentment or greed can easily color our entire emotional outlook if we do not contain it with mindfulness.

text_modern: Like a person carrying a brimful bowl of oil through a crowd of swordsmen, knowing that a single slip means death, you must maintain absolute focus as you walk the path of inner healing.

translator_notes: A classic Buddhist metaphor for radical presence. It illustrates the high level of concentration and care required to keep our minds steady and peaceful amidst chaotic external influences.

text_modern: Just as you would spring up in terror if you felt a poisonous snake slithering onto your chest, shake off lethargy and complacency the very moment you feel them creeping over you.

translator_notes: Immediate intervention. Lethargy, procrastination, and mental numbness are comfort-seeking defenses that prevent growth. We must treat them with the same urgency as a physical threat.

text_modern: Every time you falter, reflect deeply with honest regret and ask yourself: "How can I prevent this from happening again?"

translator_notes: Reflective learning instead of self-punishment. True regret is constructive; it analyzes the mistake to develop better behavioral strategies, rather than spiraling into toxic shame.

text_modern: For this very reason, seek out the company and support of wise guides, so you may learn from them how to apply mindfulness to every unique challenge in your life.

translator_notes: The importance of therapeutic community and mentorship (sangha). We cannot heal in isolation; we need wise mirrors and compassionate guides to help us navigate our blind spots.

text_modern: Keep your mind light and flexible, holding close the teachings on mindfulness, so that you are always mentally prepared and ready to act before the moment arrives.

translator_notes: Mental agility and proactive readiness. By maintaining a light, non-clinging mind, we can adapt to unexpected stressors with ease. Note 52 refers to the Dhammapada, Chapter 2 (Appamada-vagga - On Mindfulness).

text_modern: Just as a light tuft of cotton floats and dances on the gentle movements of the wind, let your actions be effortlessly carried forward by your joyful energy. This is how true, transformative power is realized.

translator_notes: Flow state and effortless effort. When the ego's resistance is dissolved and energy flows freely through compassion, action becomes lightweight, graceful, and profoundly effective, resembling magic. --- CHAPTER 8

text_modern: Having thus developed energy, focus your mind in meditative absorption; for a person with a distracted mind is caught in the fangs of the passions.

translator_notes: Meditative concentration (dhyāna) is crucial for mental stability. Without it, energy is scattered, and we easily succumb to emotional triggers.

text_modern: Physical and mental isolation eliminates distraction. Therefore, let us step back from the frantic pace of the world and quiet our endless preoccupations.

translator_notes: Creating healthy boundaries and intentional spaces for solitude is a recognized therapeutic practice to reduce cognitive overload and emotional distress.

text_modern: If we struggle to step back from worldly distractions, it is due to our deep attachments and our craving for gain or external validation. To dissolve these obstacles, the wise should reflect in this way.

translator_notes: Worldly distractions are often defensive maneuvers to avoid facing our inner voids. Identifying our attachments helps us address the root causes of our restlessness.

text_modern: It is through deep, focused quietude that the clear-minded person destroys destructive habits. Therefore, seek concentration first, knowing that it is born from letting go of worldly grasping.

translator_notes: Lasting peace is not achieved by fighting our thoughts, but by stepping out of the sensory rat race, which naturally allows the mind to settle.

text_modern: How can an impermanent, fleeting being cling so desperately to another impermanent being? For thousands of lifetimes, you may never see the object of your attachment again.

translator_notes: An honest confrontation with existential transience. Clinging to others as permanent sources of security inevitably leads to grief, as all relationships are subject to change.

text_modern: When you cannot see them, you fall into deep sadness and lose your peace of mind; and even when you are with them, you are never fully satisfied, and the thirst for their presence torments you just as before.

translator_notes: This describes the psychological mechanism of co-dependency and addictive attachment. Grasping actually prevents us from enjoying the present moment with our loved ones.

text_modern: Blinded by attachment, you fail to see reality. You lose your healthy boundaries and are consumed by sorrow, driven solely by the desperate desire to hold onto what you love.

translator_notes: Excessive attachment limits our perspective, keeping us locked in anxiety and preventing us from accepting the natural flow of life.

text_modern: Lost in this constant worry, you waste your short life hour by hour. For the sake of a fleeting relationship, you abandon the path of eternal peace.

translator_notes: Neglecting our long-term mental well-being and life purpose for the sake of temporary emotional dependencies.

text_modern: If you copy the habits of the unconscious, you will inevitably drift into pain. Yet if you try to live differently, they will resent you. What good, then, can come from seeking their constant validation?

translator_notes: Peer pressure and the desire for social conformity can keep us stuck in toxic patterns. True healing often requires the courage to walk a path that others may not understand.

text_modern: One moment they are your friends, and the next they are your enemies. In trying to please them, you only offend them; it is no easy task to satisfy those who live unconsciously.

translator_notes: Worldly relationships built on ego and convenience are inherently unstable and volatile. Relying on them for self-worth is a recipe for emotional instability.

text_modern: If you advise them toward the good, they get angry and try to pull you away from what is wholesome; if you ignore them, they get angry still and drift further into harm.

translator_notes: This highlights the limits of our ability to change others. Trying to force change on those who are unready often breeds resentment and drains our own emotional reserves.

text_modern: Jealous of superiors, hostile to equals, arrogant toward inferiors, inflated by praise, and enraged by criticism—when does a confused mind ever produce genuine good?

translator_notes: A brilliant psychological profile of the insecure, ego-driven personality. It describes the exhausting defense mechanisms of comparison, arrogance, and hypersensitivity.

text_modern: Exalting oneself, denigrating others, and wasting time in gossip about sensory pleasures—those who are confused only trade harmful habits with other confused minds.

translator_notes: How unconscious patterns are reinforced through co-rumination and superficial social interactions.

text_modern: Bringing such toxic influences together only multiplies suffering. Therefore, I will live in quiet solitude, keeping my body at ease and my heart peaceful.

translator_notes: Solitude is framed here not as lonely isolation, but as a protective, therapeutic sanctuary needed to heal and decompress from social stress.

text_modern: Avoid harmful companions from a distance. Yet if you must meet them, treat them with gentle kindness—not to form deep bonds, but to remain fair and poised, as fits a wise person.

translator_notes: Recommends keeping polite, compassionate, yet firm boundaries. We do not have to hate or reject people to protect our peace; we simply maintain an objective distance.

text_modern: Gathering only what serves your inner growth, like a bee taking nectar from flowers, pass through this world gently, without forming attachments, like a quiet new moon.

translator_notes: A beautiful metaphor for mindful consumption. We interact with the world and gather what is nourishing without consuming or being consumed by it.

text_modern: "I am rich, honored, and highly sought after!" Suddenly, death stands before the terrified mortal.

translator_notes: Worldly success and fame can easily create a false sense of security, which is instantly shattered when we face our fundamental vulnerability.

text_modern: Any object in which the mind seeks its pleasure, deceived by a false promise of happiness, eventually turns into a source of much greater pain.

translator_notes: Chasing hedonic pleasure as a cure for inner pain is a cognitive error that leads to addiction and deeper disappointment.

text_modern: If you are wise, do not chase worldly pleasures, for this search breeds danger. If pleasures arise naturally, observe them with calm clarity, without clinging.

translator_notes: The text does not forbid joy, but warns against grasping. Enjoying life's simple pleasures mindfully and letting them go without grief is the key to resilience.

text_modern: There have been so many who were wealthy and famous; yet with all their riches and glory, no one even knows who they are today. Where have they all gone?

translator_notes: Contemplating the transience of fame and power helps to put our current anxieties about status and legacy into perspective.

text_modern: Others despise me—why should I rejoice when I am praised? Others praise me—why should I grieve when I am defamed?

translator_notes: Developing emotional equanimity. When we realize that both praise and criticism are passing worldly winds, we stop outsourcing our self-worth to others.

text_modern: People have so many different preferences; not even the fully awakened ones can satisfy everyone, let alone an ordinary person like me. Why, then, should I worry about the judgments of the world?

translator_notes: An liberating cognitive shift. Realizing that it is mathematically impossible to please everyone frees us from the exhausting prison of people-pleasing.

text_modern: They mock the poor and condemn the rich. With people so difficult to live with, how can one find true peace by trying to satisfy them?

translator_notes: Worldly standards are highly inconsistent and critical. True peace must be cultivated from within, independent of external judgments.

text_modern: The Sages have said that a narrow-minded person loves no one, because they only love what serves their own self-interest.

translator_notes: Worldly love is often highly transactional. What we call "love" is frequently an projection of our own desires and needs onto another person.

text_modern: Love that is based on self-interest is nothing but self-love, just as we only mourn another's loss because of the pleasures and comfort we lose.

translator_notes: A sharp psychological truth about grief: much of our pain over loss is actually grief for our own lost comfort and security, highlighting the self-centered nature of ordinary attachment.

text_modern: The trees are neither arrogant nor difficult to get along with; when will I live among them, whose company is so gentle and easy?

translator_notes: Nature as a therapeutic co-regulator. Being in nature offers a profound sense of safety and acceptance, free from the social evaluations that trigger our insecurities.

text_modern: Living in a deserted temple, beneath the trees, or in quiet caves, when will I wander free and indifferent, never looking back?

translator_notes: Cultivating the inner freedom that allows us to walk away from toxic environments and unnecessary baggage without regret.

text_modern: In the free, expansive retreats of nature, when will I live independent, detached, and at peace?

translator_notes: Aspiring to a state of emotional self-sufficiency and deep harmony with our surroundings.

text_modern: Owning only an earthen pot and a simple robe useless to thieves, when will I live free from all fear, without even having to defend my body?

translator_notes: Voluntary simplicity. The fewer possessions and attachments we have to defend, the less anxiety we carry in our minds.

text_modern: When will I go to the cemetery, the body's natural home, to compare other corpses with my own, destined like them for decay?

translator_notes: The practice of cemetery meditation (asubha-bhavana). Facing physical decay helps us break through our obsession with appearance and physical vanity.

text_modern: Here is my body: it will become rot, and its stench will eventually drive away even the jackals.

translator_notes: Dismantling physical identification by realizing that our physical form is ultimately temporary, organic matter.

text_modern: It will lie alone; even the bones that made up its frame will scatter. How much more so will friends and family leave me?

translator_notes: Solitary departure. Recognizing that we must face the ultimate transition of death alone helps us develop inner strength and reliance on the truth.

text_modern: We are born alone and we die alone; no one can share our ultimate pain. What, then, are friends who keep us tied to illusion? Only attachments.

translator_notes: This encourages us to form healthy, non-clinging connections rather than using relationships as a desperate shield against our existential loneliness.

text_modern: Just as a traveler stops briefly at a roadside inn, so a living being stays for only a short moment in this single life.

translator_notes: Viewing life as a temporary journey, which helps us hold our current struggles, roles, and identities with a lighter, more spacious touch.

text_modern: Before the four pallbearers carry you away amidst the lamentations of your loved ones, seek the quiet sanctuary of the forest!

translator_notes: Encourages us to begin our inner healing and contemplation now, in the present, rather than waiting for the crisis of terminal illness or old age.

text_modern: Without attachment or aversion, living simply in this quiet body, already dead to worldly illusions, you will no longer fear the arrival of death.

translator_notes: When we have already let go of our false ego and worldly grasping, death has nothing left to steal from us. This is the ultimate cure for death anxiety.

text_modern: There will be no one nearby whose grief will pierce your heart, and no one to distract you from focusing your mind on wisdom and the path.

translator_notes: Finding a quiet, undisturbed space to do deep emotional and spiritual work, free from interpersonal dramas.

text_modern: Quiet solitude is beautiful and free from worry; it is highly conducive to liberation, clearing away all mental chatter. I will dedicate myself to it forever.

translator_notes: Reaffirming the profound value of silence and meditation in consolidating our mental health and processing life experiences.

text_modern: Freed from all other cares, my mind focused entirely on my thoughts, I will strive to make my mind gentle, attentive, and cooperative.

translator_notes: Mental focus allows us to observe our inner workings with curiosity and compassion, transforming the mind from a chaotic tyrant into a helpful ally.

text_modern: Blind passion is a source of suffering both now and in the future: in this life, it leads to prison, injury, and ruin; in the next, it leads to hell.

translator_notes: Uncontrolled lust and obsessive attachment are highly destructive. They drive us to make reckless decisions that ruin our lives, relationships, and peace of mind. Clean_Text: Look at these bones! For their sake, you once bowed to matchmakers, sinned without counting, risked your life, and spent your fortune. When you embraced them, you thought you were touching the peak of happiness. Now, here they are, ownerless and cold. You can embrace them now—why are you not thrilled? Context_Notes: A dramatic cognitive technique to break through sexual objectification and obsessive lust. By stripping away the superficial layers of physical attraction, we confront the raw, clinical reality of the human body. Clean_Text: This face that used to look down so modestly, hidden behind a veil, is now being uncovered by vultures who pity your desperate chase. Look at it! Why do you run away? The body you guarded so jealously from others is being eaten now. Why do you not defend it? Context_Notes: Highlights the irony of our possessiveness and jealousy over another person's body. In the end, the physical form we tried to hoard is reclaimed by nature, exposing our jealousy as an illusion.

text_modern: You see this mass of flesh being devoured by vultures and other beasts; yet you decorate this very prey with garlands, sandalwood, and jewels!

translator_notes: This points out the absurdity of physical vanity, dressing up a temporary mass of organic matter that is ultimately destined to decay.

text_modern: You shudder to look at this motionless corpse; why, then, were you not afraid of it when a living spark set it in motion?

translator_notes: Reminds us that the physical body is always the same organic matter. Our attraction to it is entirely dependent on the presence of consciousness and the illusions we project onto it.

text_modern: You loved it when it was covered, yet when it is bare, it fills you with horror. If you have no use for it now, why did you caress and pamper it when it was hidden?

translator_notes: Exposes the highly subjective and superficial nature of physical lust, which is easily shattered by simply changing the visual presentation of the same object.

text_modern: Saliva and filth have the exact same origin: food. If filth disgusts you, why do you find pleasure in tasting saliva?

translator_notes: A direct, cognitive challenge to the selective disgust of our senses, helping us see the body's secretions objectively.

text_modern: Soft cotton pillows have no charm for the lustful, because they lack the raw, physical scent that drives them mad!

translator_notes: This explains how lust is driven by unconscious biological drives and projections rather than any inherent beauty in the physical form itself. Clean_Text: If you love impurity, why embrace another frame of bones bound by tendons and plastered with flesh? Your own body is impure enough; content yourself with it, instead of seeking another vessel of filth. Context_Notes: Encourages self-reliance and self-containment. Instead of constantly seeking external physical gratification to soothe our inner restlessness, we should learn to be at peace with our own physical reality.

text_modern: You say you love this flesh and desire to see and touch it. How can you desire a physical form that is, by its very nature, unconscious?

translator_notes: Realizing that the physical body is just inert matter. True connection is spiritual and conscious, yet we often mistake physical touch for emotional intimacy.

text_modern: The consciousness you desire cannot be seen or physically touched, and the body that can be touched has no awareness of it. It is in vain that you embrace it!

translator_notes: A profound insight into the loneliness of physical lust. Physical closeness alone cannot satisfy our deep craving for true, conscious connection.

text_modern: You might overlook that another's body is made of simple organic matter; but that you do not notice your own body is just as fragile and impure is truly surprising!

translator_notes: Points out our blind spot: we are often hyper-aware of physical realities in others while ignoring our own physical vulnerability and decay.

text_modern: Ignoring the beautiful young lotus blooming under a cloudless sun, how can a mind intoxicated with craving seek pleasure in a vessel of impurity?

translator_notes: We often ignore the clean, peaceful joys of nature and wisdom, choosing instead to exhaust ourselves in the messy, anxiety-ridden pursuits of lust.

text_modern: You refuse to touch the ground if it is soiled with dirt; how then can you desire to touch the very body from which that dirt came?

translator_notes: Exposes the cognitive contradiction in our senses, showing how we arbitrarily label the same physical elements as "clean" or "dirty" based on our desires.

text_modern: If you do not love impurity, why embrace another body whose birth, seed, and nourishment are all organic and physical?

translator_notes: Grounding our romantic illusions in the raw, biological reality of physical existence.

text_modern: You have no taste for tiny worms born of decay; yet you love this body, which is also born of organic matter and composed of a vast mass of it.

translator_notes: A cognitive reframing tool to de-escalate obsessive physical attraction by comparing the body to simpler, organic life forms.

text_modern: Not only do you lack disgust for your own physical impurity, but you actively seek out other physical forms to satisfy your craving, like a scavenger!

translator_notes: A stern self-correction to shake the mind out of its addictive cycles of seeking physical gratification.

text_modern: Beautiful and fragrant things like camphor, rice, and spices become impure and repulsive the moment they are spat from the mouth onto the ground.

translator_notes: Demonstrates how the body naturally processes and alters everything it touches, reminding us of our organic, physical limits.

text_modern: If you still do not believe your body is transient and impure, go look at the hideous, cold corpses cast away in the cemeteries.

translator_notes: Recommends direct exposure to reality as an antidote to denial and vanity.

text_modern: Since the body stripped of its skin excites only deep horror, how can you, knowing this, still find your ultimate pleasure in it?

translator_notes: Encourages looking past the superficial skin-deep presentation of things to cultivate a more realistic and balanced perspective.

text_modern: If a body smells sweet, that scent comes from the sandalwood applied to it. Why cling to an object because of a perfume that is not its own?

translator_notes: Reminds us that much of what we find attractive is artificially added, warning us not to fall in love with superficial, temporary enhancements.

text_modern: If the body's natural state does not excite passion, isn't that for the best? Why do people, in love with what harms them, coat it with artificial perfumes?

translator_notes: Suggests that our natural, unembellished state is actually peaceful, and that we create our own anxiety by constantly trying to make the transient look permanent.

text_modern: What does it matter to the physical body if the sandalwood smells sweet? Why attach yourself to a form because of a scent that belongs to something else?

translator_notes: True beauty and worth are internal; physical grooming and perfume do not change our underlying character or mental state.

text_modern: If the body is covered in mud, with wild hair and long nails, and yellow, dirty teeth, its natural physical repulsiveness is plain to see.

translator_notes: Stripping away the illusions of grooming to see the physical body's raw, biological baseline.

text_modern: Why then groom and prepare it so carefully, like polishing a sword to stab yourself? The world is full of confused minds who are solely applied to deceiving themselves.

translator_notes: Warning against excessive vanity and self-objectification, which only increase our anxiety about aging and loss.

text_modern: The sight of cold skeletons in a graveyard disgusts you; yet you find pleasure in a village full of walking skeletons!

translator_notes: A powerful perspective shift: every living person we meet is simply a future skeleton. This realization softens both our lust and our social anxieties.

text_modern: And this physical body cannot even be obtained or maintained without wealth, for which we endure exhausting labor and invite the torments of mental hells.

translator_notes: Worldly desires are expensive, not just financially, but in terms of the mental and emotional toll they take on us.

text_modern: A child is unable to earn money. What will a young man have for his pleasures? His youth is spent chasing wealth, and once he is old, what use are those pleasures to him?

translator_notes: Highlights the tragic irony of the rat race: we spend our best years exhausting our health to buy pleasures, only to find we are too old and tired to enjoy them when we finally arrive.

text_modern: Some, driven by intense desires, work exhausting jobs all day, and returning home at night, lie on their beds like the dead.

translator_notes: This describes the modern reality of burnout and chronic fatigue, where we sacrifice our life force just to keep up with our cravings.

text_modern: Others go to war, suffering long, painful absences, and do not see their wives and children for years, though they claim to work for them.

translator_notes: Workaholism and obsession can isolate us from the very relationships we claim to protect and support.

text_modern: That for which they sell themselves, blinded by desire, they do not even obtain. Their lives flow away uselessly in the service of others.

translator_notes: Chasing carrots that keep moving away. Many spend their lives working for goals they never reach, wasting their precious time.

text_modern: Others sell their freedom to masters who force them to travel constantly. Their wives must give birth in jungles and deserted places.

translator_notes: Describing the high cost of financial and social dependency, where we trade our basic human dignity and family peace for economic survival.

text_modern: Others, to survive, throw themselves into battle at the risk of their lives. They seek glory and find only slavery, blind victims of their own desires!

translator_notes: This warns against chasing after empty prestige and recognition, which often ends up trapping us in exhausting roles and expectations.

text_modern: Others, because of their cravings, are stabbed, impaled, burned, or killed with spears.

translator_notes: Obsessive greed and desire inevitably lead to conflict, violence, and self-destruction.

text_modern: The worry of earning wealth, the burden of preserving it, and the grief of losing it make fortune a great misfortune. Those whose souls are bound to riches are distracted and unable to free themselves from life's suffering.

translator_notes: The psychological burden of wealth. True security is not found in accumulation, but in developing a mind that is at peace with having enough.

text_modern: Such are the miseries of those prey to desire; their petty pleasures are worth no more than the meager grass fed to an ox pulling a heavy cart.

translator_notes: A vivid metaphor for the hedonic treadmill. We work incredibly hard for tiny moments of gratification that never truly satisfy us.

text_modern: For this tiny pleasure, which even beasts can enjoy, humans, blinded by fate, throw away this rare opportunity of human life, so difficult to obtain.

translator_notes: Wasting our unique human capacity for self-awareness and healing on basic, instinctive pleasures that do not lead to long-term fulfillment.

text_modern: For this impermanent, ordinary body, destined for decay and spheres of pain, what hardships we have endured since the beginning of time!

translator_notes: Reflecting on how much energy we have wasted in past lives and habits, serving a physical form that we must ultimately leave behind.

text_modern: With a thousand times less effort, one could have achieved awakening. Slaves of desire suffer far more than Bodhisattvas, yet they achieve nothing but pain.

translator_notes: A powerful reframing of discipline. Living mindfully is actually much less painful and exhausting than living as a slave to our constant, unyielding desires.

text_modern: Swords, poison, fire, cliffs, enemies—none of these can compare to the dangers of desire, if one considers the tortures of mental hells.

translator_notes: External threats can only harm us physically, but unchecked internal cravings can utterly destroy our mental health and peace of mind.

text_modern: Therefore, fear desires and find your joy in solitude, in peaceful forests where there are no quarrels or worries.

translator_notes: Choosing to prioritize peace, simplicity, and mental hygiene over the stressful competition of worldly life.

text_modern: On beautiful rocks, spacious as palace terraces, cooled by the sandalwood of moonlight, happy is the one fanned by silent forest breezes, walking in contemplation of others' welfare!

translator_notes: A lyrical description of the deep, clean joy of meditation. True happiness is found in a quiet, spacious mind that is dedicated to helping others.

text_modern: They stay wherever they please, in an abandoned dwelling, under a tree, or in a cave; free from the worry of protecting possessions, they wander wherever they wish.

translator_notes: The psychological freedom of having nothing to lose. When we are free from attachment to status and possessions, we are truly free.

text_modern: Moving at will, without attachment, bound to no one, they taste a joy that even the king of gods, Indra, could never achieve.

translator_notes: Inner freedom is the highest wealth. Even those who rule worlds cannot taste the peace of a mind that has let go of all grasping.

text_modern: By reflecting on the excellence of solitude, silencing frivolous thoughts, let us cultivate the spirit of awakening.

translator_notes: Solitude and reflection are the fertile soil in which compassion and the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) can grow deep roots.

text_modern: First, reflect deeply on the equality of yourself and others: "Since all share the same joys and sorrows as I do, I must protect them just as I protect myself."

translator_notes: The crucial practice of the equality of self and other (paratma-samata). It is the cognitive realization that every living being feels pain and joy just as intensely as we do, breaking the illusion of our own specialness.

text_modern: The body, despite its diverse limbs, is protected as a single unit; so must it be in this world, where different beings share a common capacity for joy and sorrow.

translator_notes: Viewing humanity as a single organism. Just as the hand naturally helps the foot, we should naturally help others, recognizing that we are all part of the same interconnected whole. Clean_Text: Though another's pain does not physically hurt me, it is still difficult for them to bear because of their self-attachment, just as my pain is difficult for me to bear. Therefore, I must treat their pain with the same care. Context_Notes: True empathy. We do not have to physically feel another's pain to recognize their suffering and feel a natural responsibility to help relieve it.

text_modern: I must overcome the suffering of others because it is suffering, just like my own; I must do good to others because they are living beings, just like me.

translator_notes: Universalizing compassion. Suffering is undesirable wherever it occurs. Compassion should be based on the simple presence of pain, not on whether we personally know or like the person suffering. Clean_Text: Since we all share an equal desire to be happy, what special privilege do I have to seek only my own happiness? And since we all fear danger and pain, what privilege do I have to protect only myself and not others? Context_Notes: Challenging our innate ego-centrism. There is no logical or moral reason why our own happiness and safety should be prioritized over that of anyone else.

text_modern: "Their pain does not affect me!" Is that a reason not to protect them? The suffering of my future self does not affect me now either—why then do I take care to prevent it?

translator_notes: Exposes the illusion of the solid "self" through time. We readily work to protect our "future self" (who does not exist yet), proving that we are capable of working for someone outside our immediate, present experience.

text_modern: "Because my future self is still me!" This is an error; the one who dies is different from the one who is born.

translator_notes: From a deep psychological and Buddhist perspective, the self is a constantly changing stream of processes, not a fixed, solid entity. Caring only for "our" future stream while ignoring other streams is logically inconsistent.

text_modern: "It is up to the one who suffers to defend themselves!" Yet the hand protects the foot when it hurts, even though the pain of the foot is not the pain of the hand.

translator_notes: Shows how cooperation is already our natural state. Our body parts work together instinctively to relieve pain, and we should extend this same natural cooperation to our social relationships.

text_modern: "Though it may seem illogical, it comes from the deep habit of personal identity!" Yet all such illogic must be eliminated, whether in ourselves or in others.

translator_notes: Identifying egoism as a deeply ingrained cognitive habit. Just because we have always thought self-centeredly does not mean we cannot train our minds to think more expansively.

text_modern: "Continuity" and "aggregation" are mental fictions, like "an assembly" or "an army." There is no permanent owner of pain; who then is the one suffering?

translator_notes: A profound insight into selflessness (anatta). The "self" is a conceptual label we apply to a collection of changing physical and mental parts, just as "army" is a label for a collection of soldiers.

text_modern: All suffering is without a permanent owner; it must be dissolved simply because it is suffering. Why place arbitrary boundaries on compassion?

translator_notes: Suffering is just suffering, a natural imbalance in the universe. Our task is to relieve it wherever we find it, without dividing it into "mine" and "yours."

text_modern: "But if there is no suffering self, why fight suffering?" Because everyone agrees that suffering is undesirable. If it must be prevented, let it be prevented everywhere! If not, then let it not be prevented anywhere, not even for myself.

translator_notes: This addresses a common philosophical objection, reminding us that the lack of a solid "self" does not make pain any less real or undesirable in our direct experience.

text_modern: "But since compassion brings mental pain, why actively seek it?" Compared to the massive suffering of the world, can the temporary pain of compassion really be called great?

translator_notes: The pain of empathy is a healthy, connecting pain. It is far lighter and more meaningful than the chronic, isolating pain of keeping our hearts closed to the world.

text_modern: If the suffering of many can be resolved by the pain of one, that person should willingly accept it out of compassion for others and themselves.

translator_notes: Healthy self-sacrifice. Taking on temporary discomfort to bring lasting peace and safety to a group is a powerful act of love and leadership.

text_modern: This is why Supushpachandra, knowing well what he would suffer at the hands of the king, did not spare himself, in order to save many from despair.

translator_notes: Referencing Note 53. The story of Supushpachandra shows the ultimate courage of a Bodhisattva who prioritizes the truth and the safety of others over their own physical survival.

text_modern: Having cultivated such thoughts, finding joy in calming the pain of others, Bodhisattvas plunge into hell as easily as swans glide into a pond of lotuses.

translator_notes: A beautiful image of resilient compassion. When your heart is fully dedicated to helping others, even the most challenging environments feel like spaces of purposeful service rather than places of punishment.

text_modern: The liberation of all beings is for them an ocean of joy that drowns out everything else. Why chase a selfish, solitary peace?

translator_notes: Selfish peace is flat and isolated. True emotional and spiritual fulfillment is found in the shared joy of collective healing and connection.

text_modern: If you do something for others, do it without pride, without self-congratulation, and without wishing for a reward. Let your only passion be the welfare of others.

translator_notes: Pure altruism. When we help others without expecting praise or return, we protect ourselves from disappointment and keep our minds perfectly clean.

text_modern: Just as I protect myself from harm and dishonor, I will cultivate thoughts of protection and kindness for everyone.

translator_notes: Universalizing self-preservation. We take the natural care and concern we feel for ourselves and project it onto the entire world.

text_modern: By habit, we label drops of another's fluids—which have no independent substance—as "myself."

translator_notes: Reminds us that our physical identity is a learned habit. We were born from biological cells that were once external to us, yet we easily learned to call them "me."

text_modern: Why then can we not learn to view the bodies of others as "myself"? Recognizing our physical body as separate and external is a concept that is entirely achievable.

translator_notes: If we can learn to identify with our physical body, we can also learn to identify with the global community, expanding our circle of care.

text_modern: By recognizing that we are full of flaws while others are oceans of good qualities, we should willingly let go of our narrow self-identity and adopt the perspective of others.

translator_notes: An antidote to self-absorption. Actively looking for the good in others while remaining humble about our own flaws is a highly effective way to quiet the ego.

text_modern: We care for our limbs as parts of our body; why not care for all people as parts of humanity?

translator_notes: Re-framing humanity as our larger body, helping us see social responsibility as a natural act of self-care.

text_modern: By habit, we apply the concept of "me" to this brief, soulless body; why not apply it to others?

translator_notes: Since identity is a mental construct, we have the power to consciously expand it to include others, moving from ego-system to eco-system.

text_modern: Doing good in this way, we will feel no pride or expectation of reward. No one expects a reward simply for feeding themselves.

translator_notes: When others are seen as part of our extended self, helping them becomes as natural as eating when we are hungry, free from self-congratulation.

text_modern: Just as you naturally want to protect yourself from misery and sorrow, let this protective, compassionate care for all beings become your second nature.

translator_notes: Continuous practice transforms intentional compassion into an effortless, automatic way of being.

text_modern: This is why the Protector Avalokiteshvara has given his very name to protect people even from the minor fear of being intimidated in public gatherings.

translator_notes: Avalokiteshvara personifies active, reassuring compassion that meets people exactly where they are, alleviating even their smallest anxieties and fears.

text_modern: Do not be discouraged by the difficulty. There are things whose very names once made us shudder, but through the power of habit, we now cannot live without them.

translator_notes: Neuroplasticity and behavioral change. Habits that initially feel impossible can become natural and essential over time through consistent, gentle practice.

text_modern: Anyone who wants to quickly save both themselves and others must practice the great secret: the exchanging of self and others.

translator_notes: Exchanging self and other (paratma-parivartana). It is the core psychological practice of this chapter: mentally putting oneself in another's place to dissolve the ego. Clean_Text: Excessive self-love makes us fear the slightest danger. How can we not hate this selfish ego, which acts like an enemy, destroying nature and harming others just to satisfy its fleeting hunger? This ego only prepares our own torment in the fires of hell. Context_Notes: A stark warning against the destructive nature of narcissism and extreme selfishness, which ruins our relationships, harms society, and ultimately traps our own minds in anxiety and guilt.

text_modern: What sensible person would cherish, protect, and flatter this body, instead of treating it as a dangerous opponent to be mastered?

translator_notes: Viewing the ego-mind as an opponent to be trained, rather than a master to be blindly obeyed.

text_modern: "If I give, what will I have to eat?" This selfish grasping makes you a monster. "If I eat, what will I have to give?" This generous spirit makes you a king among gods.

translator_notes: Contrasts the psychology of scarcity (fear of not having enough) with the psychology of abundance (finding joy in sharing). Generosity expands our mind and connects us to others.

text_modern: Whoever makes others suffer for their own benefit will reap misery. Whoever takes on hardships for others will find all happiness.

translator_notes: The natural law of emotional reciprocity. Harming others isolates and poisons our own mind, while helping others builds a safe, warm internal world.

text_modern: The same ambition that causes suffering in the next world and shame in this one—if transferred to the welfare of others—produces celestial joy, honor, and wisdom.

translator_notes: Sublimation of ambition. We do not destroy our drive and energy; we simply redirect them away from selfish gain and toward serving the collective good.

text_modern: Whoever forces others to work for them will reap slavery. Whoever works for the sake of others will reap influence and respect.

translator_notes: Grasping for control and dominance over others backfires, trapping us in constant suspicion and conflict. True, lasting respect is earned through humble service.

text_modern: All those who are unhappy are so because they sought only their own happiness. All those who are happy are so because they sought the happiness of others.

translator_notes: One of the most famous and psychologically profound verses of the text. Self-absorption is the root of misery, while altruistic focus is the true source of joy.

text_modern: What more needs to be said? Just compare the fool who is entirely focused on self-interest with the wise Sage who acts solely for the benefit of others.

translator_notes: Invites us to look at real-world examples: those who are self-absorbed are usually anxious and lonely, while those who live for others carry a natural, quiet joy.

text_modern: You cannot achieve the peace of a Buddha, nor even find genuine happiness in this life, if you do not exchange your own comfort for the pain of others.

translator_notes: Our personal happiness is intimately bound up with the happiness of those around us. We cannot thrive in isolation.

text_modern: Even in this world, is our own interest not ruined if a servant refuses to work or if a master refuses to pay their wages?

translator_notes: Shows that even basic societal survival is built on cooperation and mutual support, not on raw selfishness.

text_modern: Instead of cooperating for their mutual well-being, humans only seek to harm one another, punishing themselves with deep, unnecessary suffering.

translator_notes: Exposes the tragedy of conflict. When we view others as threats rather than partners, we create a hostile world where everyone suffers.

text_modern: All the disasters, pain, and dangers of the world come from grasping at the self. Why cling to it?

translator_notes: Self-cherishing is identified as the fundamental root of all personal and systemic suffering, encouraging us to loosen our grip on the ego.

text_modern: If you do not let go of the ego, you cannot escape suffering, just as you cannot escape being burned if you refuse to step away from fire.

translator_notes: As long as we hold onto our rigid ego-identity, we remain highly vulnerable to emotional pain. Letting go of the ego is like stepping away from a fire.

text_modern: Therefore, to heal my pain and the pain of others, I surrender myself to the world and adopt others as "myself."

translator_notes: The formal resolution to practice the exchange of self and other as a primary therapeutic path.

text_modern: "I belong to others!" Let this be your firm conviction, my heart. The welfare of all beings must now be your only thought.

translator_notes: Relinquishing ownership of the self. By dedicating our life to others, we find a profound, liberating sense of purpose.

text_modern: These eyes, which belong to the world, must not look only for my benefit. These hands, which belong to others, must not move only to serve me.

translator_notes: Treating our body and mind as tools loaned to us by the universe to help relieve suffering.

text_modern: Dedicated entirely to the welfare of others, whatever useful strength you find in your body, take it and put it at the service of the world.

translator_notes: Using our talents, energy, and resources constructively for the collective good.

text_modern: By treating the humble as yourself and treating yourself as an external person, you can use your envy and pride in a wholesome, transformative way.

translator_notes: A unique psychological technique: we take our habitual ego-energies (envy, pride, comparison) and direct them against our own ego to dismantle it.

text_modern: "Why is that person treated so well, while I am not? I don't earn as much as they do! They are honored while I am ignored! I suffer while they are happy!"

translator_notes: Mentally placing yourself in the position of a disadvantaged other, looking at your own privileged self with feelings of envy and resentment to build empathy.

text_modern: "I work while they rest! They are praised for their qualities, and I am dismissed because I have none."

translator_notes: Deepening the role-reversal, experiencing the pain of social inequality from the outside to break through our own entitlement.

text_modern: "But is anyone truly devoid of qualities? Everyone has their own. I may be inferior to some, but I am superior to others."

translator_notes: Realizing our shared humanity and value, reminding ourselves that everyone we meet has their own unique worth. Clean_Text: "If my virtue or understanding is lacking, it is the force of habit and passions, not my true will. I will undergo the discomfort of healing. If this ego judges me incurable, why does it look down on me? What use are its qualities if they only serve its own pride?" Context_Notes: Exposing the cruelty of the ego's internal critic. The ego often uses comparison to make us feel worthless, which only prevents our healing.

text_modern: "They have no compassion for the poor suffering in hell, yet in their pride, they claim to surpass the wise!"

translator_notes: Criticizing our own ego's lack of empathy, exposing its coldness and self-satisfaction.

text_modern: "If they meet an equal, they struggle to surpass them; they will start quarrels just to satisfy their greed and ambition."

translator_notes: Shifting perspective to look at our own competitive, aggressive habits from the outside, recognizing how destructive they are to relationships.

text_modern: "May my qualities enjoy universal fame, and may theirs remain completely unnoticed!"

translator_notes: Giving voice to our shadow self's petty, hidden desires for fame and recognition, exposing them to the light of awareness.

text_modern: "May my flaws stay hidden, and may all honors come to me while they get none! Now I have won; I am honored, and they are forgotten."

translator_notes: Laying bare the absolute selfishness of the unobserved ego, which helps us realize how desperately we need to train our minds.

text_modern: "Let us rejoice to see them finally humbled, mocked, and defamed everywhere."

translator_notes: Exposing the ugly, envious parts of our shadow self to conscious observation, which naturally weakens their hold on us.

text_modern: "Look at this miserable person who dared to rival me! What do they have? They lack knowledge, wisdom, beauty, noble birth, and wealth."

translator_notes: Confronting our ego's arrogance and elitism by giving them a voice, making us highly aware of our own judgmental habits.

text_modern: Hearing the qualities of the "Ego" praised everywhere, I will leap with joy and taste a delicious satisfaction.

translator_notes: Observing our craving for validation and praise from an objective distance.

text_modern: If the "Other" possesses any wealth, we will take it by force, leaving them just enough to survive, so long as they serve us.

translator_notes: Exposing the raw, exploitative drives of the self-absorbed mind, helping us realize how we unconsciously treat others as mere tools for our convenience.

text_modern: We must pull them down from their happiness and transfer our pain onto them. A hundred times we have suffered because of this selfish ego.

translator_notes: This captures the tragic core of trauma transmission: we often try to escape our own pain by inflicting it on others. Realizing this motivates us to stop the cycle.

text_modern: You have spent countless lifetimes chasing your own self-interest, and what did you gain? Nothing but pain.

translator_notes: An honest evaluation of our history. Selfishness has never brought us lasting peace or happiness; it has only kept us locked in conflict and anxiety.

text_modern: Obey this training without hesitation. You will see its immense benefits later, for the words of the wise are infallible.

translator_notes: Encouraging us to trust the therapeutic process, even when it feels counter-intuitive to our defensive instincts.

text_modern: If you had practiced this rule earlier, you would not be in this painful state today, and you might have already attained the supreme peace of a Buddha.

translator_notes: Reframing past regrets as motivation to start practicing mindfulness and compassion today.

text_modern: Therefore, just as you transferred the concept of "me" to drops of fluids that were once foreign to you, realize it now in others.

translator_notes: Reinforcing the idea that since our identity is fluid and learned, we can consciously train ourselves to expand our circle of care.

text_modern: Be a guardian of others: watch this body, and whatever strength you find in it, direct it to serve the world.

translator_notes: Treating our own body as a tool that has been loaned to us to do good work in the world.

text_modern: "This person is comfortable, while that one is in pain. This one is high, while that one is low. That one works, while this one idle." Turn your jealousy inward, against your own selfish ego.

translator_notes: Sublimating jealousy. Instead of envying others, we turn that critical focus inward to dismantle our own complacency and egoic habits.

text_modern: Cast your own comfort aside, take on the hardships of others, and constantly watch the tricks of your selfish mind.

translator_notes: Actively choosing to step out of our comfort zone to serve others, which builds deep emotional resilience.

text_modern: Take responsibility even for the mistakes of others, and be quick to expose even your smallest flaws to the light of awareness.

translator_notes: Moving away from defensiveness and blame. Taking responsibility is a powerful act of agency that fosters deep, relational healing.

text_modern: Speak lightly of your own reputation while exalting the good name of others. Treat your ego like a servant dedicated to the needs of all.

translator_notes: Letting go of the exhausting need to defend our reputation, finding freedom in simple, quiet service.

text_modern: Since the ego is naturally flawed, do not praise it for minor, temporary virtues. If it has good qualities, keep them quiet.

translator_notes: Practicing quiet humility. We do not need to advertise our goodness; the joy of helping is its own complete reward.

text_modern: In short, all the harm you once did to others for your own benefit, turn it around: take on their burdens for their benefit.

translator_notes: Resolving to live with a focus on reparation and healing, actively correcting our past self-centered habits.

text_modern: Do not allow your ego to dominate or chatter arrogantly. Train it to be modest, humble, and respectful, like a quiet guest.

translator_notes: Cultivating a quiet, non-obtrusive presence, which naturally makes our relationships more peaceful and harmonious.

text_modern: "Do this! Hold yourself like that! Do not do that!" This is how you must bend your ego to your will, correcting it when it slips.

translator_notes: Active self-discipline. We treat our ego like a wild animal that needs gentle, consistent, and firm training to become helpful.

text_modern: "And if you do not obey me, my mind, I will punish you, you who are the container of all my flaws!"
