translator_notes: Establishing clear, internal boundaries against our own toxic patterns. We refuse to let our mind slide back into destructive habits.

text_modern: "Where do you think you are going? I see right through you! I will crush your pride. The days when you could ruin me are over."

translator_notes: Developing a strong, observing self. By seeing our defense mechanisms clearly, we stop them from unconsciously running our lives.

text_modern: "Give up all hope of pursuing selfish interest today. I have dedicated you to the world, and I will not indulge your complaints."

translator_notes: Commitment to our values. We refuse to let the ego's temporary discomforts and complaints distract us from our larger purpose.

text_modern: "If I made the mistake of not giving you to others, you would undoubtedly hand me over to the torment of my own mental hells."

translator_notes: Realizing that self-cherishing is a trap. If we do not actively work to overcome our ego, it will inevitably lead us back to anxiety and isolation.

text_modern: "How many times have you already dragged me into misery? What long suffering I have endured! Remembering your hostility, I now master you, servant of selfishness!"

translator_notes: Shaking off the victim mindset. We reclaim our agency and refuse to let our old, unconscious habits dictate our emotional state any longer.

text_modern: If you truly wish to care for yourself, stop indulging yourself. If you want to protect yourself, do not coddle your ego.

translator_notes: The paradox of self-care. True self-care is not soft indulgence; it is the firm, compassionate discipline needed to build a healthy, resilient mind.

text_modern: The more you pamper the physical body, the more fragile and demanding it becomes.

translator_notes: Over-indulgence lowers our window of tolerance, making us hypersensitive to minor discomforts and easily thrown off balance.

text_modern: And even then, the entire earth would not be enough to satisfy its endless cravings. Who would want to be a slave to such desires?

translator_notes: Cravings are inherently insatiable. Trying to find peace by satisfying every desire is like trying to put out a fire with gasoline.

text_modern: Those who chase after the impossible only harvest anxiety and disappointment. But those who are free from grasping enjoy an unshakeable peace.

translator_notes: Peace is not the presence of fulfilled desires, but the absence of grasping.

text_modern: Therefore, do not allow physical cravings to grow unchecked. Realize that what is wholesome is that which is free from grasping.

translator_notes: Learning to enjoy life with a light touch, appreciating things as they are without needing to possess them.

text_modern: The body is a temporary, impure form that ends in ash. It is inert, moved only by a brief spark. Why cling to it as "mine"?

translator_notes: Softening physical identification. Realizing our physical transience helps us hold our physical self with more humor and less anxiety.

text_modern: What use is this physical machine, living or dead? How is it different from a mound of earth? Oh, ego, why do you not let go?

translator_notes: A direct invitation to let go of our rigid physical identity, reminding us of our deep connection to the earth and elements.

text_modern: My blind favoritism for my body has brought me nothing but anxiety. It is as simple as a block of wood—why worry about its likes or dislikes?

translator_notes: Realizing that much of our suffering comes from our stories about comfort, rather than the physical sensations themselves.

text_modern: Whether I pamper it or let the elements reclaim it, it feels neither love nor hate. Why should I invest my peace in it?

translator_notes: The physical body has no opinion on vanity. Our anxiety about aging and appearance is entirely a mental construct that we can choose to let go of.

text_modern: I get angry when it is mistreated and happy when it is praised. But since the physical body itself knows nothing of this, why do I exhaust myself over it?

translator_notes: Exposes the empty nature of physical vanity and pride, helping us step out of the exhausting search for physical validation.

text_modern: "But those who care for this body are my friends!" Yes, but everyone cares for their own body. Why should I not treat everyone with the same warm friendship?

translator_notes: Expanding our circle of connection. Just as we instinctively appreciate those who help us, we can learn to appreciate everyone, recognizing our shared vulnerability.

text_modern: Therefore, I surrender my attachment to this body for the sake of the world. If I maintain it, despite its flaws, it is only as an instrument for helpful action.

translator_notes: Redefining our relationship with our body. It is no longer an idol to be worshipped, but a helpful tool to be used for doing good work in the world. Clean_Text: Leave behind all superficial ways! I will follow the path of the wise. Remembering the teachings on mindfulness, and overcoming laziness and fatigue, I will dismantle my inner obstacles. I will pull my mind back from harmful paths and bring it home to its true refuge. Context_Notes: A strong, final resolution. We commit to mindful presence, letting go of the ego's distractions and bringing our mind home to its natural state of peace and compassion. --- CHAPTER 9

text_modern: All these auxiliary virtues are taught by the Sage for the sake of wisdom. Therefore, one must cultivate wisdom if they desire the complete ending of suffering.

translator_notes: Wisdom (prajñā) is the ultimate goal of the entire Bodhisattva path. The previous chapters (charity, moral discipline, patience, energy, concentration) are preparatory phases designed to purify and prepare the mind for this absolute realization.

text_modern: There are two truths: the relative truth of appearance, and the absolute truth of reality. Absolute reality lies beyond the reach of the conceptual mind, for the mind itself belongs to the realm of relative appearances.

translator_notes: This introduces the Madhyamaka Two Truths doctrine: relative truth (samvriti-satya) which functions conceptually, and absolute truth (paramartha-satya) which is non-conceptual, direct insight into the emptiness of all phenomena. Clean_Text: Correspondingly, there are two kinds of people: the meditative contemplatives and ordinary worldly people. The contemplatives see deeper than ordinary people, and they form a hierarchy based on the clarity of their insight. Yet, both groups can communicate through shared metaphors to reach the ultimate goal. Context_Notes: Distinguishes between worldly perception and meditative insight (yogis vs. ordinary beings). Although they perceive differently, language and everyday analogies are used by the wise as a bridge to guide others toward non-conceptual truth.

text_modern: Ordinary people perceive things as solidly real, rather than as fleeting illusions. This is the fundamental difference in perspective between worldly minds and contemplatives.

translator_notes: Worldly minds suffer because of a cognitive bias that attributes permanent, intrinsic reality to changing, dependent phenomena (reification). Contemplatives view all things as empty and dream-like.

text_modern: Sensations and physical forms seem real through common sense, not because of logical proof. But common sense is mistaken, just as it mistakenly judges an impure body to be pure.

translator_notes: Common sense and physical perception are unreliable guides to ultimate reality. They are bound by cognitive illusions, such as mistaking transient, composite bodies for pure, permanent, desirable entities.

text_modern: The Master taught the existence of objects merely as an introduction to emptiness, not as the absolute truth. If objects were truly momentary, as some believe, this momentariness would still belong to the relative realm, not the ultimate.

translator_notes: Refuting the Abhidharma (early Buddhist) view of momentary atomic dhammas. Even momentariness is a conceptual construct used as a stepping stone to help the mind transition toward complete emptiness (śūnyatā).

text_modern: There is no error in the relative truth as long as it aligns with insight. Compared to ordinary minds, the contemplatives see closer to the truth. For instance, even in common life, you deviate from the masses by recognizing that the physical form is fundamentally impure.

translator_notes: Relative truth is valid within its functional context. The meditative view of physical impurity, while still relative, is closer to the truth because it counteracts the destructive delusion of physical attachment. Clean_Text: "If all things are empty, then the Buddha is merely an illusion. What merit can come from honoring him?" The merit is exactly the same as if his existence were solidly real. "But if a being is merely an illusion, how can they die and be reborn?" An illusion lasts as long as the causes that produce it; that an illusion appears as a continuous stream does not mean it exists in reality. Context_Notes: Addresses the nihilistic misunderstanding of emptiness. Even though the Buddha is conceptually "empty" of independent existence, honoring him produces positive psychological and karmic effects because the causal stream of relative reality still functions.

text_modern: "If it is all an illusion, then there is no sin in killing an illusory human, since they have no real consciousness." No, because the act is committed against a being who appears to have consciousness; therefore, relative merit and demerit are still generated.

translator_notes: Emptiness does not mean moral nihilism. Ethics operate fully within the realm of relative truth, where suffering and intention are functionally real and carry real psychological consequences. Clean_Text: "A conscious illusion is impossible; even magic cannot create a mind." But illusions take many forms and arise from different conditions; a single cause does not have to produce every kind of illusion. Context_Notes: Defending the possibility of empty, illusory consciousness. Just as a physical illusion is born of visual trickery, conscious experience is born of mental conditioning. Clean_Text: "If beings exist only as illusions, then does the Buddha also transmigrate?" As long as the causes of an illusion are not cut, the illusion continues to appear; but once the causes are cut, the illusion ceases, even in the relative realm. Context_Notes: Transmigration (samsara) is a continuous stream of illusory conditioning. Nirvana is achieved not by destroying a real self, but by cutting the causes (craving, ignorance) that keep the illusion going. Clean_Text: "If nothing is real, not even the mind that perceives, who is it that perceives the illusion?" But if for you the illusion itself does not exist, then what is it that you perceive? Context_Notes: Beginning of the refutation of the Yogācāra (Vijñānavāda) school of idealism, which holds that while external objects are empty, the dualistic mind itself exists truly. Madhyamaka argues that the mind is just as empty as its objects (Note 54). Clean_Text: "It is a form of the mind, appearing different from reality." But if the illusion is the mind itself, then who is the seer and what is seen? For the Buddha said: "The mind cannot see the mind; the spirit is like the edge of a sword, which cannot cut itself." Context_Notes: Refutes self-cognizing consciousness (svasamvedana). Consciousness cannot be its own object, just as a sword cannot cut its own blade or a finger cannot touch its own tip. Clean_Text: "The mind illuminates itself, just like a lamp." But a lamp does not illuminate itself, for it is never in darkness to begin with. Context_Notes: Refuting the lamp analogy. Light does not need to illuminate itself because darkness is never present in light. Therefore, the mind cannot be said to "see" itself in a dualistic way. Clean_Text: "We mean that the mind is naturally self-luminous. The color blue, for instance, does not depend on another blue to be blue, unlike clear crystal." But blue is not independent, for it cannot make itself blue if it is not already so. We can observe that a lamp illuminates; but who can observe and prove that the mind illuminates itself? Whether the mind is dark or luminous, if it is never seen by anyone, talking about it is as meaningless as describing the beauty of a child born to a barren woman. Context_Notes: This dismantles the concept of an intrinsically real, self-aware mind. Every phenomenon, including the mind, exists interdependently; nothing exists in and of itself.

text_modern: "But if there is no self-awareness, how do we remember what we experienced?" Memory arises through association with external objects and conditions, just as a hibernating animal is triggered by the return of spring.

translator_notes: Explains memory without needing an independent self-cognizer. Memory is a relational process of association and conditioning, analogous to how delayed symptoms of a latent poison (Note 55) manifest later under specific conditions.

text_modern: "Since we can see another's mind through clairvoyance, can we not see our own?" No, for the magical ointment that reveals a hidden treasure is not the treasure itself.

translator_notes: Experiencing states of mind does not prove the existence of an independent, self-existent soul or mind-entity.

text_modern: We do not deny the practical reality of sensory experience, memory, or intelligence; but we reject the claim that they possess absolute, independent existence, for this belief is the root of all suffering.

translator_notes: Crucial distinction: Madhyamaka is not nihilistic. It accepts everyday functional reality (sensations, thoughts) but refutes the cognitive error of reification (attributing intrinsic, permanent selfhood to them).

text_modern: If you claim that the illusory object is different from the mind, it is false; if you claim it is identical to the mind, it is also false. If it exists in reality, how could it be identical to the mind? If it is identical to the mind, how is it real?

translator_notes: Demolishes the dualistic separation and identity of mind and object. Both arise dependently; they cannot be strictly identical or entirely separate. Clean_Text: Though the illusory object does not truly exist, it is still seen; and though the mind does not truly exist, it still perceives. Context_Notes: The mystery of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). Reality functions beautifully and dynamically precisely because it is empty of solid, permanent existence. Clean_Text: If you claim that this unreal world of suffering rests upon a truly real mind, then the world must be entirely separate from the mind, as empty as space. Furthermore, how can an unreal thing act upon or be supported by a real mind? In your system, the mind is left with nothing but void. And if the mind has no object, then all beings are already awakened. What, then, is the purpose of practicing virtue if nothing exists but pure, isolated mind? Context_Notes: Points out the logical dead-ends of absolute idealism. If the mind is truly real and independent, it cannot relate to or perceive an unreal world. Emptiness must apply to both subject and object.

text_modern: "But even if we understand that the mind is illusory, how does that eliminate passion? Does not a magician still fall in love with the magical woman he created?"

translator_notes: A practical, therapeutic question: How does intellectual understanding of emptiness actually help us overcome deep-seated emotional attachments and addictions?

text_modern: "Yes, because the magician has not yet destroyed the underlying habit of believing in the reality of objects. When he looks at his creation, his understanding of emptiness is too weak to override his biological triggers."

translator_notes: Intellectual knowledge is not enough. Cognitive habits and emotional triggers are deeply ingrained. We need deep, meditative integration of emptiness to decondition our habitual emotional responses. Clean_Text: But when you are fully saturated with the realization of emptiness, the illusion of solid existence vanishes. By repeatedly seeing that nothing has intrinsic reality, even the concept of emptiness itself eventually dissolves. Indeed, when you no longer construct the illusion of a solid self, the concept of "non-self" also fades away. When neither existence nor non-existence presents itself to the mind, the mind, free from any conceptual hook, finally rests in perfect peace. Context_Notes: The ultimate therapeutic de-reification. Emptiness is not a dogma to cling to, but a medicine. Once the sickness of grasping is cured, the medicine of "emptiness" must also be let go, leaving the mind in pristine, non-conceptual peace.

text_modern: Just as the wish-fulfilling jewel and the tree of dreams fulfill wishes without intention, the body of the Buddha appears spontaneously in the world through his past compassionate vows and the spiritual needs of his disciples.

translator_notes: Explains how an awakened being acts effortlessly and without ego. The Buddha's activity is a spontaneous, non-conceptual response to the suffering of the world, like a natural law. Clean_Text: Just as a snake charmer can die after consecrating a magical pillar, and that pillar continues to neutralize venom long after his death; so too, this "Pillar of the Victor," established through the practice of the Bodhisattva path, continues to heal and guide beings long after the Teacher has entered perfect peace. Context_Notes: Reassures practitioners of the ongoing power of the teachings and the lineage. The wholesome influence of a wise, compassionate life echoes through time, acting as a supportive structure for others even after that life has ended. Clean_Text: "How can honoring an unconscious, departed Buddha produce results?" Because the scriptures state that honoring a living Buddha and honoring a departed Buddha are equal, yielding the same fruits whether viewed from relative or absolute truth. If honoring an empty illusion were not fruitful, then how could honoring a "real" Buddha be so? Context_Notes: The transformative power of devotion and archetypes. Honoring the qualities of the Buddha (wisdom, compassion) works as a psychological mirror, awakening those same qualities within our own minds.

text_modern: "We achieve liberation by seeing the Four Noble Truths; what is the purpose of meditating on emptiness?" Because the scriptures state that ultimate awakening cannot be achieved without this path.

translator_notes: Emptiness (Note 56) is not an optional philosophical study; it is the essential experiential insight needed to completely dissolve the subtle roots of egoic grasping and achieve total freedom.

text_modern: "But the Mahayana teachings are not proven!" And your own scriptures, how are they proven? "Because we both accept them." They were not accepted before you existed; therefore, your own standard is inconsistent.

translator_notes: Addressing sectarian debates. The validity of a spiritual path is proven by its therapeutic results—its capacity to dissolve suffering—not by consensus or dogmatic authority.

text_modern: The same faith you place in your own scriptures should be extended to the Mahayana. If the validity of a truth depended solely on the agreement of non-believers, then we would have to accept the Vedas and all other worldly texts as absolute.

translator_notes: Demands intellectual consistency and open-mindedness. Every spiritual tradition has its own internal validity; we must judge a path by its fruits.

text_modern: "But the Mahayanists themselves disagree!" Then abandon your own scriptures too, for every school is in disagreement not only with other traditions, but even with its own members and sub-sects.

translator_notes: Intellectual disagreement is a natural part of human inquiry. Internal debates do not invalidate the core therapeutic efficacy of the teachings.

text_modern: True spiritual life is rooted in liberation. Yet liberation is incredibly difficult for those whose minds still cling to the solid reality of conceptual objects.

translator_notes: Clinging to any concept—even spiritual ones—as solidly real acts as a barrier to ultimate freedom. True liberation requires a radical letting go of all conceptual grasping.

text_modern: "If liberation comes from merely destroying obvious passions, then an Arhat should be completely free immediately." Yet we see that even those who have quieted their raw passions can still act out of subtle conditioning.

translator_notes: Distinguishes between removing obvious emotional distress (klesha-avarana) and dissolving the subtle, unconscious cognitive biases and habits of dualistic perception (jñeya-avarana).

text_modern: "But they no longer have craving or attachment!" We deny this; for is there not a subtle form of craving, born of intellectual confusion, that remains even when obvious passions are quieted?

translator_notes: Even when we do not feel active greed or anger, a subtle, unconscious grasping at a solid self and a solid world still persists, which can trigger suffering under the right conditions.

text_modern: Craving arises from sensation, and sensations are still experienced by the saints. As long as the mind perceives objects as solidly real, it will naturally grasp at them.

translator_notes: Sensation is a natural physiological process. But if we have not realized emptiness, our minds will automatically overlay these sensations with stories of "me" and "mine," triggering craving.

text_modern: Without the realization of emptiness, the bound mind will always find something to cling to, just as a person in deep, unconscious sleep still carries latent conditioning. Therefore, let us cultivate emptiness.

translator_notes: Emptiness is the only solvent strong enough to dissolve the deepest, unconscious layers of egoic grasping, ensuring that the mind does not slide back into suffering.

text_modern: "But if the realization of emptiness dissolves all fear and attachment, won't it also dissolve our motivation to stay in this world and save others?" No, for compassion itself operates as a beautiful, wise illusion to relieve the real pain of others.

translator_notes: (Verse 50-52 are noted as interpolations by Finot's commentary and skipped). This addresses the "compassion paradox." Realizing that beings are empty of solid selfhood does not destroy compassion; rather, it purifies it, making it selfless, fearless, and incredibly effective.

text_modern: Therefore, this criticism of emptiness is completely unfounded. Let us cultivate emptiness without any hesitation.

translator_notes: Emptiness is not a threat to love and compassion; it is the very freedom that allows love to become boundless, unconditional, and fearless.

text_modern: Emptiness is the ultimate cure for the mental blindness caused by toxic passions and our rigid beliefs about the world. If you desire complete clarity and peace, why delay cultivating it?

translator_notes: Emptiness is the ultimate cognitive reframe, dissolving the mental distortions that warp our perception of ourselves and others.

text_modern: It is logical to fear what causes pain; but emptiness actually pacifies all pain. Why, then, do you fear it?

translator_notes: Many people fear emptiness because they mistake it for cold, depressing nihilism. In reality, emptiness is the open, spacious freedom that allows all healing to occur.

text_modern: "It is natural to feel fear as long as you believe you are a solid, vulnerable self. But for the one who realizes, 'I am not a solid self,' what is there left to fear?"

translator_notes: Beginning of the refutation of Materialism. If there is no solid, separate "I" to protect, then all existential anxiety, fear of loss, and fear of death naturally dissolve. Clean_Text: I am not the teeth, the hair, the nails, or the bones. I am not the blood, the mucus, the phlegm, or the pus. I am not the saliva, the sweat, the fat, or the organs. I am not the waste, the tendons, the body heat, or the physical openings, nor am I the six sensory perceptions. Context_Notes: A systematic, body-scan meditation designed to deconstruct our physical identification. By looking at each component objectively, we realize that "I" cannot be found in any of these physical parts.

text_modern: If our hearing were a permanent, independent self, then we would hear sounds constantly. If there is no sound to be heard, how can you speak of hearing or a self?

translator_notes: Beginning of the refutation of the Sāṃkhya philosophy, which posits a permanent, conscious Self (Purusha/Atman). If the Self is permanent hearing, it would hear sound continuously even in silence, which is a logical absurdity.

text_modern: If you claim that the self remains conscious even without an object, then a block of wood would also be conscious. Therefore, it is clear that there can be no consciousness without an object to be aware of.

translator_notes: Consciousness is always intentional; it is always "consciousness of" something. An independent, permanently conscious self that doesn't depend on objects is a conceptual fiction.

text_modern: "Why does the self, while looking at a physical form, not hear a sound?" You might say it is because no sound is present. But then, in that moment, the self cannot be called "hearing."

translator_notes: Shows the fluid, dependent nature of our experience. Our identity shifts with our sensory focus; there is no single, permanent self running the show. Clean_Text: How can that which is by nature visual perception suddenly become auditory perception? You might imagine that the same person can be both a father and a son, but that is merely a conceptual relationship, not an absolute truth. If you believe only in the reality of the three primal qualities of nature, then there is ultimately neither father nor son. Context_Notes: Refuting Sāṃkhya's theory of the three primal qualities (Guṇas: Sattva, Rajas, Tamas). Conceptual roles (like father and son) are relative and relational, not absolute, self-existent entities. Clean_Text: "When the self is hearing a sound, its visual nature is simply unmanifested. It assumes a different nature to see form, just like an actor changing roles on stage." Context_Notes: The opponent's counter-argument: the self is a single actor that changes manifest qualities. Clean_Text: "But then, in your system, the same self must possess two completely different natures at once. This is an unheard-of kind of unity!" Context_Notes: Pointing out the logical contradiction. If the self changes its very nature, it cannot be called "permanent" or "unitary."

text_modern: "If you say that these changing roles are unreal, then tell us what the real, permanent nature of the self is. Is it simply the capacity to know? But then all human beings would be the exact same, single entity!"

translator_notes: If "knowing" is the sole, uniform nature of all selves, then there would be no separation between different individuals, rendering personal identity meaningless.

text_modern: "And you would even have to admit that conscious beings and unconscious objects are identical, since they both share the quality of existence. If all individual differences are dismissed as unreal, what is left to support your claim of a personal identity?"

translator_notes: Pushes the opponent's logic to its absurd extreme, showing that a permanent, homogeneous self-concept destroys the very differences it tries to explain.

text_modern: "The self is not naturally unconscious, like a piece of cloth. It becomes conscious only through its union with consciousness." But if the self is naturally unconscious, then the moment it is separated from consciousness, it is completely destroyed!

translator_notes: Refutation of the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika view of a naturally unconscious soul (Atman) that temporarily connects with consciousness. If it is naturally unconscious, it cannot be a conscious self.

text_modern: "You reply that the self is permanent and unchangeable. But if it is unchangeable, what effect could its union with consciousness possibly have on it? By this logic, we might as well call empty space a 'self'!"

translator_notes: If the self is truly permanent and unchangeable, it cannot be modified by experiences, thoughts, or consciousness. An unchangeable soul is as useless and inert as empty space.

text_modern: "But how can we explain the law of cause and effect (karma) without a permanent self? If the person who acts disappears, who is left to experience the results of that action?"

translator_notes: A common psychological and ethical anxiety: if there is no solid "me," how can we maintain moral responsibility or experience the fruits of our efforts?

text_modern: "We both agree that the act and its fruit occur at different times and have different immediate supports. Since you claim the self is permanent and inactive anyway, debating this is completely unnecessary."

translator_notes: Points out that a permanent, inactive soul cannot perform actions or experience results anyway. Therefore, the concept of a soul does not help explain karma.

text_modern: "The one who acts is the one who experiences the results." This is not literally true. When the Buddha spoke of the actor experiencing the fruit, he was simply referring to the continuous stream of cause and effect under a convenient, conventional name.

translator_notes: Karma functions not because of a solid, permanent soul, but because of a continuous, changing stream of cause and effect (like a flame passing from candle to candle). The "self" is just a useful label for this stream.

text_modern: Neither the past mind nor the future mind can be the self, for they do not exist right now. Can the present mind be the self? But as soon as the present moment passes, that mind vanishes, and with it, your self would disappear.

translator_notes: Dismantling the mind-as-self. The mind is a rapid, continuous stream of moments. No single moment of mind can be a permanent self, for each moment arises and ceases instantly.

text_modern: Just as a banana tree has no solid core when you peel away its layers, the self, when examined with critical awareness, is revealed to be entirely empty.

translator_notes: A classic metaphor for emptiness. When we look closely at our thoughts, physical parts, and feelings, we find layer after layer of conditions, but no solid, independent "core" inside.

text_modern: "If there is no real individual, then on whom do we practice compassion?" We practice compassion toward the conventional concept of beings, an illusion we adopt for the sake of the ultimate goal.

translator_notes: Addresses the fear of losing compassion. We do not need a solidly real self to feel compassion. We feel compassion for the experience of suffering in conventional beings, using this "wise illusion" to guide them to freedom.

text_modern: "But whose goal is it, if the individual does not exist?" It is true that our efforts are guided by an illusion; but because this illusion has the sole purpose of ending suffering, it is a healthy, necessary tool.

translator_notes: Pragmatic use of concept. In therapy, we use concepts and goals to guide healing, even though we know these concepts are temporary tools, not absolute realities.

text_modern: The belief in a solid self, on the other hand, breeds nothing but pain and feeds our illusions. Because this belief can only be dissolved by its antidote, we must cultivate the deep realization of selflessness.

translator_notes: Self-cherishing is a harmful delusion that causes anxiety, greed, and isolation. Realizing selflessness (emptiness of self) is the necessary antidote to find ultimate psychological freedom. Clean_Text: The body is not the feet, the legs, or the thighs. It is not the hips, the belly, the back, or the chest. It is not the arms, the hands, the sides, or the armpits. It is not the shoulders, the neck, or the head. What, then, is this "body"? Context_Notes: Deconstructing the concept of the physical body. We use the label "body" for convenience, but when we look for a single, independent entity called "body" among our physical parts, it cannot be found.

text_modern: If the body exists partially in all its limbs, then we are looking at parts within parts. But where is the "body" itself, separate from these parts?

translator_notes: A logical analysis showing that the "whole" does not exist as an independent entity separate from its constituent parts.

text_modern: And if the body exists fully and completely within each individual limb, then you would have as many separate bodies as you have limbs!

translator_notes: Shows the absurdity of claiming that the "whole" is fully present in every single part.

text_modern: The body is found neither inside nor outside. How could it be in the limbs? And it is not found separate from the limbs either. How, then, can it be said to exist on its own?

translator_notes: The body exists only as a dependent, relational concept. It has no independent, self-existent reality.

text_modern: Therefore, there is no independent "body" in reality. It is only because of a conceptual illusion that we project the idea of a "body" onto a collection of limbs, just as we might mistake a wooden post for a human being in the dark.

translator_notes: Cognitive projection. Our mind automatically groups parts together and labels them, mistaking our conceptual projection (the label) for an absolute, independent physical reality.

text_modern: As long as a certain collection of conditions is present, we look at a post and see a human; in the same way, as long as a collection of parts is present in the limbs, we see a "body."

translator_notes: Explains how conventional reality functions. Concepts are valid and useful as dependent designations, but they are not absolute, independent truths.

text_modern: In the same way, there is no "foot," for it is only a collection of toes. A "toe" is only a group of joints, and a "joint" is made of smaller parts.

translator_notes: Infinite deconstruction. Every object can be broken down into smaller components; there is no solid, indivisible baseline to be found.

text_modern: These parts can be broken down into atoms, and an atom can be divided into six spatial directions. Since each direction is divisible, the atom is nothing but empty space. Therefore, there is no such thing as a solid, indivisible atom.

translator_notes: Refuting the atomic theories of the Vaiśeṣikas (Note 58). Since anything physical occupies space, it must have parts (front, back, left, right) and is therefore divisible. Ultimate, indivisible physical building blocks do not exist.

text_modern: Thus, all physical form is like a dream. What wise person would cling to it? And since the body does not exist as a solid reality, what is "man" or "woman"?

translator_notes: Dissolving gender and physical attachment. Realizing that physical forms are empty, fluid projections allows us to let go of our obsessive attachments and superficial biases.

text_modern: If suffering existed as a solid, independent reality, why does it not affect those who are in a state of joy? And why does delicious food fail to bring pleasure to someone who is consumed by deep grief?

translator_notes: Shows that feelings (pleasure and pain) are not absolute properties of objects, but are dependently arisen mental states that depend on our current conditioning and focus.

text_modern: "Perhaps the pleasure or pain is still present, but it is simply blocked and overshadowed by a stronger sensation." But how can you call something a "sensation" if you do not actually feel it?

translator_notes: Sensation requires awareness. If a feeling is not felt, it does not exist as a functional sensation, proving that sensations have no independent, unperceived existence.

text_modern: "Perhaps the pain still exists in a subtle, latent state, and its active form has been temporarily suppressed." But in that case, this "subtle pain" is nothing but a concept of potential, not a real, felt sensation.

translator_notes: Refutes the Sāṃkhya theory of latent states. A feeling is only real when experienced; a "latent feeling" is just a conceptual expectation.

text_modern: If pain does not manifest in the presence of its opposite, is it not clear that what we call "sensation" is merely a subjective projection of our own imagination?

translator_notes: Our emotional and physical experiences are highly subjective, shaped by how we interpret and focus our minds, rather than being solid, unchangeable realities.

text_modern: This is why we develop this critical analysis: to act as an antidote to our rigid mental projections. For meditators find their true nourishment in the quiet contemplations born in the spacious field of a clear mind.

translator_notes: Meditation uses deliberate focus to deconstruct our painful mental habits, replacing toxic cognitive distortions with spacious, peaceful awareness.

text_modern: If sensation is born of contact between the organ and the object, and they are separated by space, how can they touch? And if there is no space between them, they are a single unit—how then can there be contact?

translator_notes: A deep, logical analysis of sensory contact. If subject and object are entirely separate, they cannot touch; if they are identical, there is no separate subject to perceive. Sensory contact is a dependently arisen illusion.

text_modern: An atom cannot penetrate another atom, for an atom has no hollow space or inequalities. Without penetration, there is no mixing, and without mixing, there is no real contact.

translator_notes: Dismantling physical contact at the atomic level, showing that physical "touching" is a conceptual interpretation of forces, not an absolute, solid joining of matter.

text_modern: How can there be contact between things that have no physical parts? If you claim that partless things can touch, show us a single example of such a thing!

translator_notes: Logical refutation of the contact of partless, indivisible entities.

text_modern: Consciousness, having no physical form, cannot touch anything. Physical objects cannot touch either, since they have no solid, independent reality, as we have already demonstrated.

translator_notes: The mind-body connection is not a physical touching of two solid substances, but a seamless, dependently arisen co-emergence of mental and physical processes. Clean_Text: Without real contact, how is sensation even possible? And if sensation is not real, what are we struggling so hard for? Where does suffering come from, and who can it actually reach? Since there is neither a solid, suffering self nor a real sensation, why, oh thirst of desire, do you not dissolve right now? Context_Notes: A powerful therapeutic release. Realizing that both the trigger (the object) and the receiver (the self) are empty of solid reality immediately cools the heat of our cravings and anxieties.

text_modern: We see and we touch, but these experiences are creations of the mind, which is itself like an illusion or a dream. Therefore, sensation does not exist as a solid, absolute reality.

translator_notes: Compares our sensory experience to a dream. In a dream, we feel real pleasure and pain, yet when we wake up, we realize those experiences had no solid, external existence.

text_modern: Our past and future perceptions are merely memories, not present sensations. A sensation cannot perceive itself, nor can it be perceived by another separate sensation.

translator_notes: Shows the fleeting, ungraspable nature of time and experience. We cannot hold onto a sensation, for it vanishes the moment it arises.

text_modern: There is no independent subject to feel the sensation; therefore, sensation has no self-existent reality. Since this entire bundle of experience is empty of a solid core, who is there to be oppressed by it?

translator_notes: Emotional liberation. When we realize there is no solid "me" inside to be wounded, our painful emotions lose their hook and dissolve into the open space of awareness.

text_modern: The mind is found neither in the sensory organs, nor in their objects, nor in the space between them. The mind is found neither inside the body, nor outside, nor anywhere else.

translator_notes: We cannot locate the mind as a physical object in space. It is a dynamic, non-physical process of experiencing, not a "thing" hidden inside the brain.

text_modern: That which is found neither in the body, nor elsewhere, neither combined nor isolated—that has no solid existence of its own. This is why all beings are, by their very nature, already in a state of perfect peace.

translator_notes: This points to our innate sanity and peace (Tathāgatagarbha / Buddha-nature). Beneath our temporary, conceptual confusion, our minds are naturally quiet, empty, and peaceful (Parinirvāna). Clean_Text: If awareness existed before its object, what did it rely on to arise? If awareness and its object arise at the exact same time, what support does awareness have? And if awareness arises after its object, where could it possibly come from? Therefore, the independent arising of any mental event is impossible. Context_Notes: Demolishes the idea of an independent, self-contained mind or object. They arise together in mutual dependence; neither can exist without the other.

text_modern: "If nothing exists on its own, then relative appearance itself does not exist. How then can there be two truths? And if this relative world is created by another illusion, how can beings ever achieve peace?"

translator_notes: The opponent's worry: if everything is empty, then even the path to peace must be an illusion, making liberation impossible.

text_modern: "A being in peace exists through the conventional understanding of others, not through their own illusion. When we trace the chain of cause and effect, we find relative appearance; if the cause is cut, the appearance ceases."

translator_notes: Liberation is conventional. We use conventional practices (the path) to cut conventional suffering. When the illusion of grasping is cut, suffering ceases, which we conventionally call Nirvana.

text_modern: Conceptual thinking and the objects of thought rely entirely on one another. All critical analysis and everyday communication depend on these relative, shared agreements.

translator_notes: Language and logic are relational tools. They do not describe absolute, independent realities, but they are highly effective for navigating daily life and guiding us toward healing. Clean_Text: "But if our analysis of things must also be analyzed, we enter an endless loop of analysis." No, because once we have thoroughly analyzed and dissolved the object of grasping, the analysis itself has nothing left to analyze. Lacking any support, the conceptual mind naturally settles into perfect stillness. This is what we call Nirvana. Context_Notes: The therapeutic end of overthinking. We do not need an infinite loop of logic. Once we have used analysis to dissolve our rigid beliefs and cognitive distortions, our analytical mind naturally goes quiet, leaving us in serene, non-conceptual peace. Clean_Text: Anyone who believes in the absolute, independent reality of both subject and object is in a logically impossible position. If the object depends on our awareness, how do we explain awareness? If awareness depends on the object, how do we explain the object? If they both depend on each other, neither can exist on its own. For example, if there can be no father without a son, how can the son be born in the first place? Without the son, there is no father; therefore, neither exists independently. Context_Notes: Mutual dependence (pratītyasamutpāda) is the middle way. Things do not exist in and of themselves; they exist only in relation to other things, like father and son, or subject and object.

text_modern: "A plant grows from a seed, and the seed is revealed by the existence of the plant. Why can a mind born from an object not prove the independent existence of that object?"

translator_notes: The opponent tries to use the seed-and-plant analogy to prove that mutual dependence still allows for independent, objective existence.

text_modern: "Because we can verify the existence of a seed through a perception other than the plant itself. But what independent awareness can you use to verify the existence of the mind, which would then prove the existence of the object?"

translator_notes: Refutes the analogy. We cannot step outside of our own awareness to objectively verify that our awareness and its objects exist independently. Everything is experienced within the field of dependent awareness.

text_modern: Ordinary people, relying on simple perception, see that causes are complex. The division of a lotus into stem, petals, and stamens arises from a complex web of different conditions.

translator_notes: Even in everyday life, things do not arise from a single, magical source, but from a rich, complex web of natural causes and conditions.

text_modern: What is the origin of this variety of causes? It is the variety of previous causes. And why does a specific cause produce a specific result? Because of the influence of the cause that came before it.

translator_notes: The universe is a continuous, beginningless stream of cause and effect. There is no need to invent a single, absolute first cause to explain the complexity of life.

text_modern: "God is the ultimate cause of the world." Tell us, what do you mean by "God"? If you simply mean the natural elements, we agree! There is no need to argue over a mere name.

translator_notes: Beginning of the refutation of Deism/Theism (Ishvara). If "God" is just a label for the natural, physical elements of the universe, then we are simply using different words for the same natural processes.

text_modern: But these elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—are multiple, changing, unconscious, and lacking divine will. They are fragile and impure; therefore, they cannot be a supreme, intelligent God.

translator_notes: If God is defined as the physical elements, then God is unconscious, subject to change, and fragmented, which contradicts the definition of a supreme, unchanging, conscious creator.

text_modern: Space is not God, for space is inactive. The permanent soul has already been refuted. If you say God is completely beyond human conception, then his act of creation is also beyond conception—so what is the point of speaking about him?

translator_notes: Dismantling conceptual projections of a creator. If a deity is entirely beyond logic and comprehension, we cannot logically claim that he is the "creator," making the argument meaningless. Clean_Text: What could God have possibly desired to create? The soul? But you claim the soul is eternal. The elements? They are eternal by nature. Himself? He is also eternal. Knowledge? It arises from the object known. Pleasure and pain? They arise from our own actions. What, then, is left for him to create? Context_Notes: If all components of the universe are either eternal or arise dependently from their own causes (like karma), there is no logical role or need for a creator deity. Clean_Text: If the cause has no beginning, how can the effect have a beginning? Context_Notes: If the creator is eternal and unchanging, his creation should also be eternal and unchanging. An unchanging cause cannot suddenly decide to produce a new, temporal effect.

text_modern: Why would God not create everything all the time? He does not need to wait for anyone else, for there is no being who was not created by him—so who could he possibly be waiting for?

translator_notes: If a creator is all-powerful and independent, all his creations should exist simultaneously and permanently, rather than arising and passing away gradually.

text_modern: If you say he must wait for the right combination of conditions, then he is not the sole cause. He cannot create when those conditions are missing, and he cannot stop creating when they are present.

translator_notes: If the creator depends on external conditions to act, then he is not all-powerful or independent; the conditions themselves are the true causes of creation.

text_modern: If God acts without desiring to do so, it means he is dependent on something else. If he acts because he desires to, he is dependent on his own desire—and if he is dependent, what becomes of his supreme power?

translator_notes: Shows that even desire implies a lack or a dependency, which contradicts the concept of an absolutely self-sufficient, all-powerful being. Clean_Text: Those who claim that physical atoms are eternal and uncaused have already been refuted earlier. Context_Notes: Refers to the refutation of indivisible atoms (Verse 87). Physical matter is composite and dependently arisen; it cannot be eternal or uncaused. Clean_Text: The Sāṃkhya philosophers claim that primal matter is the eternal cause of the world, composed of the perfect balance of the three qualities. They say the world is born when this balance is disrupted. Context_Notes: Refuting Sāṃkhya dualism, which posits a primal, unconscious matter (Prakriti) made of three qualities (Guṇas) as the source of all physical and mental phenomena.

text_modern: A single, indivisible entity cannot have a triple nature; therefore, your primal matter cannot exist. In the same way, the three qualities themselves cannot exist independently, for each of them is also made of three parts.

translator_notes: Exposes the logical contradiction of Sāṃkhya. Something cannot be a single, unified first cause if it is made of three distinct, conflicting qualities.

text_modern: If these three qualities do not exist, then sounds and other objects of the senses cannot exist either. Furthermore, it is impossible for emotions like pleasure, pain, or confusion to exist inside unconscious objects, like clothing.

translator_notes: Feelings of pleasure or pain are subjective mental experiences, not physical properties hidden inside physical objects like clothes.

text_modern: If you claim that objects are the cause of pleasure because of their nature, we have already shown that objects have no independent existence. For you, the pleasure itself is the cause, not the clothing.

translator_notes: Dismantles the reification of pleasure. We project "pleasure" onto objects, but the pleasure is a mental reaction, not a physical substance inside the object. Clean_Text: In daily life, pleasure is experienced in relation to the clothing; if the clothing is missing, there is no pleasure. Context_Notes: Reinforces dependent origination: pleasure arises from the relation between the mind, the organ, and the object; it does not exist independently in any of them. Clean_Text: We never experience a permanent, unchanging state of pleasure. If pleasure existed constantly in a manifest state, why do we not feel it all the time? And if you say it retreats into a subtle, unmanifest state, how can something be both manifest and unmanifest? Context_Notes: Shows the transience of emotional states. Feelings are fluid, temporary processes, not permanent substances that hide and show themselves. Clean_Text: If pleasure leaves its manifest state to become subtle, then both states are impermanent. Why not simply admit that everything that exists is impermanent? If the manifest state is not different from the pleasure itself, then pleasure is clearly impermanent. Context_Notes: Accepting impermanence (anicca). Trying to find a permanent substance behind changing experiences is a cognitive distortion. True peace comes from accepting change. Clean_Text: "But something that does not already exist can never be born, for it has no reality." Yet you are forced to admit that the manifest state of pleasure is born, even though it did not exist just a moment before. Context_Notes: Refuting the Sāṃkhya theory of satkāryavāda (that the effect already exists in the cause). Real change is possible precisely because things are empty of fixed, unchangeable identity. Clean_Text: "If the effect is already fully present inside the cause, then anyone eating rice is actually eating waste, and you should buy cotton seeds instead of clothes to wear." Context_Notes: A humorous, practical reductio ad absurdum showing that causes and effects are distinct phases in a process of change, not identical substances. Clean_Text: "You might say that ordinary people do not see this because of their ignorance." But this is also the case with your own philosophers! Context_Notes: Academic and philosophical theories can often be just as delusional and disconnected from practical reality as ordinary ignorance.

text_modern: "But ordinary people also have the capacity to perceive; why do they not see things as they truly are?" Because the perception of ordinary people is not a reliable guide to absolute truth; otherwise, even the fleeting appearance of things would be an absolute reality.

translator_notes: Worldly perception is functional for daily life, but it is not an authority on the ultimate nature of reality, as it is warped by deep-seated cognitive biases.

text_modern: "If our everyday ways of knowing are not reliable, then the concepts they produce are false—and therefore, your own analysis of emptiness must also be false."

translator_notes: The opponent's counter: if all relative tools are flawed, then the concept of emptiness itself must be invalid.

text_modern: "If we do not first suppose the existence of an object, we cannot conceive of its non-existence. Therefore, if the solid existence of things is false, then their solid non-existence is obviously false as well."

translator_notes: Emptiness is not a solid "nothingness." It is the lack of independent, fixed existence. Emptiness itself is empty of independent reality; it is simply a tool to dissolve our projections.

text_modern: When a person dreams that their child has died, the false idea of the child's non-existence dissolves the false idea of the child's existence—even though both ideas are ultimately empty of reality.

translator_notes: A powerful metaphor for cognitive restructuring. In therapy, we use concepts (which are conventional constructs) to dissolve our painful, false beliefs (which are also constructs), leading to peace. Clean_Text: This critical analysis reveals that nothing exists in its causes taken separately, nor does it exist in them taken together. Nothing comes from elsewhere, nothing stays, and nothing disappears. How, then, does this world differ from a magical illusion that ordinary minds mistake for solid reality? Context_Notes: All phenomena are dependently arisen (pratītyasamutpāda). They appear dynamically when conditions come together, but they have no solid, independent starting point, duration, or end.

text_modern: What is created by magic and what is created by natural causes—where does it come from, and where does it go? This is what we must contemplate.

translator_notes: Encouraging us to look closely at the empty, dream-like nature of our experiences, which frees us from taking our temporary dramas too seriously.

text_modern: Something that appears only when other conditions are present, and vanishes when they are gone—this artificial, dependent event is like a reflection in a mirror. How could it possess any absolute, independent reality?

translator_notes: Metaphor of the mirror reflection. The reflection is vivid and functional, yet it has no independent existence separate from the mirror, the object, and the light. Clean_Text: If a thing already exists in reality, why would it need a cause? And if a thing does not exist at all, why would it need a cause? Describing causes cannot alter absolute nothingness. What is in a state of non-existence cannot be made to exist—for how could such a thing transition into reality? Context_Notes: Deconstructing causation. If things had fixed, unchangeable identities, change would be impossible. Emptiness is the very space that allows for change, healing, and growth. Clean_Text: If the real object is not present during the state of non-existence, when will it be born? For non-existence cannot disappear until the object is born, yet the object cannot be born until non-existence has disappeared. Context_Notes: Pointing out the logical paradox of treating "existence" and "non-existence" as two solid, mutually exclusive substances. Clean_Text: In the same way, a real object cannot simply turn into nothingness, for that would mean a single entity would have to possess two completely opposite natures at once. Context_Notes: A solid, independent thing cannot change its nature. Change is only possible because things are empty of fixed, independent selfhood. Clean_Text: Therefore, there is neither absolute destruction nor absolute existence. This universe knows neither ultimate birth nor ultimate death. The destinées of all beings are like a dream, like a hollow banana tree. There is no absolute, independent difference between those who are in Nirvana and those who are not. Context_Notes: Non-duality of Samsara and Nirvana. Ultimate peace is not a physical place we go to after escaping a real world; it is the direct realization of the empty, peaceful nature of this very experience. Clean_Text: Since all things are empty of solid reality, what is there to receive or to lose? Who is there to be honored or despised, and by whom? Where could pleasure or pain possibly come from? What can be truly pleasant or offensive? What is this thirst of craving, and where can we find this craving when we search for its true nature? Context_Notes: The ultimate emotional release. Realizing the emptiness of all conceptual dualities dissolves our grasp on pride, resentment, craving, and anxiety, leaving us in a state of natural freedom.

text_modern: When we examine this world of living beings, who is it that dies? Who will be born, and who has been born? Who is truly a stranger, and who is a friend?

translator_notes: Dismantling our rigid social divisions. We realize that our categories of "friend," "enemy," and "stranger" are temporary, relative projections, allowing us to feel an open, equal love for all. Clean_Text: Let us understand, my companions, that everything is as open and spacious as the sky. Yet, we continue to fight, celebrate, and anger ourselves over illusions. Seeking only our own happiness, we spend our lives in anxiety, conflict, and despair, wounding one another in endless, self-created miseries. Context_Notes: A compassionate lament over the tragedy of human ignorance. We suffer because we take our conceptual illusions too seriously, fighting over passing shadows instead of resting in our shared, open nature. Clean_Text: Beings fall into painful states to endure long, searing torments, only to return occasionally to temporary joys. This cycle of conditioned existence (Samsara) is full of constant downfalls; nothing is less stable. Everything in it is a contradiction; it cannot be an absolute reality. Context_Notes: Describes the emotional volatility of an untrained mind, constantly swinging between temporary highs and painful lows, trapped in a unstable loop of its own making. Clean_Text: It contains vast, terrifying oceans of self-created suffering. It is a realm of fragile strength and brief lives. There, we quickly waste our precious days in the struggle to survive, battling hunger, illness, fatigue, and physical accidents, while lost in empty relationships with those who are confused. In such chaos, it is incredibly difficult to cultivate clear awareness. Where can we find the space to quiet our habitual distractions? Context_Notes: A realistic look at the difficulties of human life. Our time is short, and our environment is full of distractions and stressors. This highlights the urgent need to prioritize mindfulness and emotional healing before our opportunity passes. Clean_Text: There, the force of delusion constantly tries to drag us down. The paths to suffering are many, and our confusion feels overwhelming. It is so rare to find the perfect conditions for practice, to meet a wise guide, and to quiet the torrent of our passions. Oh, what a continuous stream of pain! Context_Notes: Acknowledges the immense challenge of breaking free from generational trauma and deep cognitive conditioning, urging us to cherish and make use of our current opportunity for growth. Clean_Text: How deeply we must pity these suffering beings, swept away by the torrent of their own pain, completely blind to their own condition and only making their misery worse! They are like someone who, after bathing in water, immediately jumps into a fire to get warm, only to burn themselves even more. Context_Notes: Compassion for the self-destructive habits of humanity. We often try to escape our pain using methods that only create more pain (like addiction, anger, or isolation), like jumping into a fire to dry off.

text_modern: Living as if they will never grow old and die, they are suddenly caught completely off guard by terrible disasters, with death heading the march.

translator_notes: Exposes our denial of impermanence. We live unconsciously, ignoring our vulnerability, until crisis or loss suddenly forces us to confront reality unprepared.

text_modern: When will I be able to bring comfort to these people tormented by the fire of suffering, pouring down cool rains of peace from the cloud of my own positive mental energy? When will I be able to gently teach the wisdom of emptiness to those who cling to solid illusions, guiding them to cultivate virtue free from the prison of grasping?

translator_notes: A beautiful, compassionate aspiration. The realization of emptiness does not make us cold or detached; it fills us with an urgent, loving desire to share this liberating peace with a suffering world. --- CHAPTER 10

text_modern: By the virtue I have accumulated through composing this Guide to the Bodhisattva Way, may all human beings adorn themselves with the compassionate practice of the Bodhisattvas!

translator_notes: This is the formal act of Dedication (pariṇāmanā). It is a vital practice in Buddhist psychology to redirect any personal merit, pride, or achievement outward for the welfare of others, preventing the ego from co-opting spiritual progress.

text_modern: May all those in every corner of the world who suffer from physical or mental pain obtain vast oceans of comfort, joy, and peace through my merit!

translator_notes: A universal therapeutic wish. It aims to soothe both the somatic (physical body) and psychological (mental distress) aspects of human suffering.

text_modern: As long as they remain in the cycle of conditioned existence, may their happiness never suffer any eclipse! May they continuously experience the supreme joy of the Bodhisattvas!

translator_notes: Rather than wishing for an abrupt escape from life, the author wishes that beings find joy and resilience within their ongoing life processes (samsara), transforming their experiences from within.

text_modern: May all beings trapped in the hell realms of every world enjoy the pure delights and ultimate happiness of the land of Sukhāvatī!

translator_notes: Sukhāvatī is the Amitabha's Pure Land (Note 50), symbolizing a state of mind free from fear, distress, and trauma. The wish is to instantly transition minds in torment to a state of absolute psychological safety.

text_modern: May those freezing in the cold hells find soothing warmth, and may those burning in the hot hells be cooled by the boundless waters poured from the great clouds of the Bodhisattvas!

translator_notes: Metaphorical cooling and warming. In psychological terms, this represents regulating extreme emotional states: warming those frozen in depressive isolation and cooling those burning in the heat of rage and agitation.

text_modern: May the terrifying forest of razor-sharp leaves turn for them into a garden as beautiful as the paradise of the gods, and may the thorny trees of torture be transformed into wish-fulfilling trees!

translator_notes: Refers to Note 59 (Nandana park) and Note 36 (Kûṭaçâlmalî trees). This represents the cognitive transformation of trauma: changing environments of pain and punishment into spaces of beauty, safety, and nourishment.

text_modern: May the realms of torment become filled with the charm of clear lakes, echoing with the joyful songs of water birds and sweet with the scent of blooming lotuses!

translator_notes: Replacing internal chaos and intrusive thoughts with soothing, sensory-rich landscapes of tranquility, facilitating deep neural and emotional co-regulation.

text_modern: May the mounds of burning coals turn into heaps of precious gems! May the scorching ground become a cool pavement of crystal, and may the crushing mountains become celestial palaces filled with awakened teachers!

translator_notes: This represents transforming existential dread and crushing guilt ("crushing mountains", Note 37) into experiences of precious wisdom and protective, therapeutic sanctuaries.

text_modern: May the rains of burning coal, hot stones, and weapons turn henceforth into showers of sweet flowers! May the violent clashes of weapons become playful battles of blossoms!

translator_notes: Transformative imagery: converting external attacks, abuse, and conflict into opportunities for soft, compassionate, and playful connection.

text_modern: May those submerged in the boiling, painful river of torment, their flesh torn and their bones exposed like jasmine, obtain a radiant, celestial form through the power of my merits, and play freely in the pure waters of heaven with divine companions!

translator_notes: Refers to Note 60 (Vaitaranî, Mandâkinî, Apsaras). A profound wish for somatic healing and emotional restoration. It visualizes the complete repair of shattered, traumatized bodies into states of light, play, and community.

text_modern: May the terrifying wardens of death, the horrible crows and vultures, suddenly look up in awe as the darkness is everywhere dissolved, asking: "What is this sweet, beautiful, and delicious light?" And raising their eyes, may they see the radiant, courageous Vajrapāṇi standing in the sky, feel instantly freed from all negativity, and fly to join him in joyful haste!

translator_notes: The dissolution of fear-projections. The terrifying figures of guilt and punishment (Yama's messengers, Note 21) are transformed by the light of courage and mindfulness (Vajrapāṇi / Vajrin, Note 23), leading to a release of internalized shame.

text_modern: And look! A shower of lotuses falls, mixed with fragrant water; oh, what joy! The fires of torment are completely extinguished. "What is this?" cry those in pain, suddenly flooded with relief. It is the arrival of Padmapāṇi—may they see him standing before them!

translator_notes: Padmapāṇi (Avalokiteshvara) represents unconditional, cooling compassion. His arrival brings instant relief to the burning heart, extinguishing the fires of acute anxiety and distress.

text_modern: "Comrades!" they cry. "Come, come quickly! Cast away all fear! We are restored to life! Look, there comes a young prince wearing ribbons, bringing peace to this dark place. The power of his presence dissolves all disasters, making torrents of joy flow. The mind of awakening is born, and with it, Compassion—the mother who protects all beings!"

translator_notes: Refers to Note 61 (Cîrî kumârah / Mañjuśrī). The birth of bodhicitta (awakening mind) and compassion is celebrated as the ultimate savior, restoring life and meaning to minds lost in depression and trauma.

text_modern: "Look at him! Upon the lotuses of his feet shine the crowns of hundreds of bowing gods; his eyes are moist with deep pity; upon his head falls a rain of flowers from beautiful palaces where thousands of divine singers celebrate his praise. It is Mañjughosha! Seeing him before them, let those in torment acclaim him!"

translator_notes: Mañjughosha (Mañjuśrī) represents active, sharp wisdom. Seeing wisdom clearly cuts through our illusions of isolation and hopelessness, inspiring us to honor our own innate capacity for clarity.

text_modern: Through my merits, may those in torment have the joy of seeing Samantabhadra and all the other Bodhisattvas—clouds that pour down healing rain and stir up fresh, fragrant, and delightful breezes!

translator_notes: The archetypal Bodhisattvas (Note 13) function as positive psychological resources. Their presence brings soothing comfort, emotional cooling, and a sense of profound, loving protection.

text_modern: May the searing agonies and panic of those in torment be completely quieted! May all those trapped in painful, destructive destinies be set entirely free!

translator_notes: A direct prayer for the alleviation of acute anxiety, panic attacks, and traumatic flashbacks, wishing that all minds find safety and liberation from their habitual cycles of distress.

text_modern: May animals cease to devour one another! May the hungry ghosts be as completely satisfied and happy as the people of the mythical northern continent!

translator_notes: Refers to Note 62 (Pretas/hungry ghosts) and Uttarakuru. This is a wish for the ending of systemic violence (animals devouring each other) and the healing of chronic psychological scarcity and insatiable hunger (the Preta state).

text_modern: May the hungry ghosts be fully satisfied! May they be bathed and refreshed by the streams of pure milk flowing from the compassionate fingers of Avalokiteśvara!

translator_notes: The milk flowing from Avalokiteshvara's fingers is a powerful symbol of unconditional, nurturing love that meets our deepest, most desperate deficits, soothing our core wounds of neglect and emotional hunger.

text_modern: May the blind see; may the deaf hear; and may pregnant women give birth without any pain, just like Queen Māyā!

translator_notes: Māyā Devī was the Buddha's mother, who gave birth effortlessly. This is a compassionate wish for physical healing, the opening of sensory awareness, and the safe, trauma-free transition of new life into the world.

text_modern: May all people receive abundant clothing, food, drink, garlands, sandalwood, and jewels—everything that brings comfort to their hearts and serves their genuine well-being!

translator_notes: Acknowledges that physical security and sensory comfort are necessary foundations for mental health and spiritual practice. We cannot expect people to find peace if their basic human needs are neglected.

text_modern: May those who are afraid find courage; may those who grieve find joy; and may those whose minds are scattered and troubled find perfect stillness and peace!

translator_notes: A beautiful therapeutic wish addressing the three major emotional challenges: fear (anxiety), grief (depression), and mental agitation (distraction), bringing courage, joy, and stillness.

text_modern: May the sick regain their health; may the captive find their freedom; may the weak be filled with strength, and may all people feel a warm, mutual affection for one another!

translator_notes: Wishes for systemic healing, physical recovery, social liberation, and relational harmony. It highlights that true well-being is both personal and deeply relational.

text_modern: May every path be safe and propitious for travelers, protecting them and helping them succeed in all their journeys!

translator_notes: A metaphor for life's transitions. We wish that everyone who is navigating change, seeking direction, or moving through unfamiliar emotional terrain finds safety and guidance.

text_modern: May those who sail upon the waters achieve all their desires! May they return safely to port and rejoice with their loved ones!

translator_notes: Represents navigating the unpredictable waters of emotion and life circumstances. We wish that they survive the storms of life and return home to safe, nourishing relationships.

text_modern: May travelers lost in the wild jungles meet a helpful caravan, and may they journey without fatigue, safe from the dangers of thieves and wild beasts!

translator_notes: Being "lost in the jungle" is a metaphor for existential confusion, depression, or panic. Meeting a caravan represents finding a supportive therapeutic community or supportive group that guides us back to safety.

text_modern: May protective spirits guard those who sleep, those who are mentally ill, those who are careless, the abandoned, the weak, and the elderly, in all the dangers of sickness and the forest!

translator_notes: A deeply compassionate wish for the most vulnerable members of society—the sleeping, the mentally ill, the neglected, and the elderly—asking that they be held in a field of universal protection and care.

text_modern: May all people be free from setbacks, endowed with robust faith, wisdom, compassion, pleasant appearances, and mindful conduct, remembering their past lives!

translator_notes: Wishing for the integration of mental clarity, physical vitality, ethical integrity, and deep psychological continuity (remembering past lives, which represents processing and integrated memory).

text_modern: May they possess inexhaustible treasures, like Gaganagañja; may they live in perfect harmony, rest, and independent freedom!

translator_notes: Note 63 (Gaganagañja). True abundance is an open, spacious mind that is free from the anxiety of lack, allowing us to live in peaceful, non-clinging harmony with others.

text_modern: May those who are sluggish and lacking energy be filled with enthusiasm! If they feel unattractive, may they be filled with natural beauty!

translator_notes: Overcoming lethargy and low self-esteem. True beauty is the radiant glow of a peaceful, compassionate mind that feels worthy and loved.

text_modern: May all women achieve the strengths of the male form! May those who are humble be raised up, yet remain completely free from pride!

translator_notes: In the historical context, wishing for the male form represented wishing for social agency and freedom from patriarchy. Today, this represents empowerment, equal agency, and social justice, combined with genuine humility.

text_modern: Through the power of my merits, may all beings without exception turn away from harmful actions and continuously practice what is wholesome and good!

translator_notes: A wish for universal ethical transformation. When we understand the causes of suffering, we naturally choose to align our actions with kindness and wisdom.

text_modern: May they never be separated from the mind of awakening; may they apply themselves diligently to its practice, guided by the wisdom of the Buddhas and protected from the traps of delusion!

translator_notes: "Mâra" is the personification of delusion, temptation, and cognitive distortion. The wish is that we remain anchored in our values, protected from falling back into unconscious, toxic habits.

text_modern: May all beings enjoy a limitless life! May they live in continuous happiness, and may the very name of death disappear from their minds!

translator_notes: Wishing for the dissolution of the fear of death by helping minds rest in the timeless, unborn nature of pure awareness.

text_modern: May all regions of space be filled with Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, made beautiful by parks of wish-fulfilling trees, and enchanted by the sweet sound of the Dharma!

translator_notes: Transforming our entire perception of reality. When our minds are purified, we no longer see the world as a hostile battlefield, but as a sacred space of learning, beauty, and wisdom.

text_modern: May the earth be everywhere smooth and free from gravel and sharp stones, level like the palm of a hand, soft, and filled with precious gems!

translator_notes: Smooth ground represents the smoothing out of our psychological obstacles, trauma, and friction, allowing us to walk through life with ease, softness, and grace.

text_modern: May vast assemblies of Bodhisattvas gather everywhere, decorating the earth with their radiant presence.

translator_notes: Visualizing a world filled with supportive, compassionate mentors and peers, creating a healthy and co-regulating social environment.

text_modern: May the birds, the trees, the beams of light, and the sky itself constantly echo the voice of the truth to the ears of all!

translator_notes: Everything in our environment becomes a teacher of truth when we learn to listen mindfully. The natural world is constantly reflecting the laws of impermanence and interconnectedness.

text_modern: May all people live in the constant presence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, honoring the Teacher of the World with clouds of beautiful offerings!

translator_notes: Maintaining a continuous, conscious connection with our highest values and archetypes of wisdom, keeping our hearts open and devotional.

text_modern: May the rains fall in their proper seasons; may the harvests be rich and abundant; may the world be prosperous, and may leaders govern with justice and fairness!

translator_notes: A wish for environmental stability, economic security, and just leadership, recognizing that systemic justice is essential for collective well-being.

text_modern: May all plants be highly effective medicines; may helpful formulas succeed, and may the spirits, demons, and negative forces be filled with pity and kindness!

translator_notes: Wishes for effective healing tools and the pacification of negative, hostile forces (demons/Dâkinîs, Note 35), transforming conflict into understanding.

text_modern: May no being ever be unhappy, suffering, sick, abject, defeated, or filled with malice!

translator_notes: A beautiful, all-encompassing wish for the absolute eradication of physical, emotional, and social suffering, hoping that every mind is filled with health and peace.

text_modern: May the monasteries be flourishing sanctuaries of study and practice! May harmony reign within the community, and may its helpful work succeed!

translator_notes: Wishing for the health and integrity of healing communities and spiritual spaces, ensuring they remain safe, supportive places for learning and growth.

text_modern: May those who practice cultivate deep discernment and find joy in their study! May they meditate with a diligent mind, completely free from distraction!

translator_notes: Encouraging mental hygiene and focused attention. Meditation is most effective when approached with a playful, curious, and disciplined mind.

text_modern: May those in monastic life receive abundant support, free from conflict and worry! May all practitioners observe their ethical rules with perfect care!

translator_notes: Wishes for the safety, financial security, and moral integrity of those who dedicate their lives to spiritual and psychological training.

text_modern: May those who have faltered be moved to heal their hearts, actively clearing away their mistakes! May those who are faithful to their vows reach the supreme state of awakening!

translator_notes: Compassionate restoration. We do not judge or exile those who make mistakes; we support them in their process of repair, self-forgiveness, and growth.

text_modern: May they be wise, well-mannered, honored with gifts, supported by the kindness of others, pure in character, and known for their quiet goodness throughout the world!

translator_notes: Wishing that spiritual practitioners embody integrity, kindness, and humility, serving as gentle, trustworthy mirrors for the community.

text_modern: Without having to endure the torments of hell, and without a painful, exhausting struggle, may all people achieve awakening in a single, radiant body!

translator_notes: A wish for the most direct, gentle, and trauma-free path to healing. True awakening does not require unnecessary suffering; we can heal through gentleness and grace.

text_modern: May all the Awakened Ones be honored in every way by all living beings, and may they rejoice in their inconceivable, supreme happiness!

translator_notes: Honoring the archetype of the fully healed mind, wishing that the presence of wisdom and peace remains vibrant and celebrated throughout the world.

text_modern: May the compassionate vows made by the Bodhisattvas for the sake of the world be fully accomplished! May the wishes of these Protecters be realized for all beings!

translator_notes: Aligning our personal efforts with the cosmic, archetypal force of compassion, wishing that all selfless projects for healing succeed.

text_modern: May the solitary realizers and disciples be happy, always honored with respect by gods, forces, and humans!

translator_notes: Respecting different paths to peace. Whether one seeks quiet, individual healing (Note 50) or collective transformation, all sincere efforts toward peace deserve our respect.

text_modern: May I remember my past lives and obtain the State of Joy forever, through the grace of Mañjughosha!

translator_notes: Note 64 (Pramuditabhûmi / State of Joy). The first major stage of the Bodhisattva path is characterized by overwhelming joy born of selflessness and connection.

text_modern: In whatever posture or situation I spend my time, may I maintain my inner strength! In all my lives, may I obtain complete clarity and discernment!

translator_notes: A prayer for resilience and mindfulness. We wish to stay present, strong, and clear, no matter what external challenges or physical postures we find ourselves in.

text_modern: Whenever I desire to see him or ask a question, may I see my protector Mañjughosha standing before me without any obstacle!

translator_notes: Wishing for instant, direct access to our own inner wisdom whenever we face confusion, doubt, or crisis.

text_modern: Just as Mañjuśrī walks in the ten directions and to the very ends of the sky for the benefit of all, may I also carry out my life's journey for the sake of the world!

translator_notes: Setting Mañjuśrī (the embodiment of active, compassionate wisdom) as our ultimate model for how we show up and move through the world.

text_modern: As long as space remains, and as long as the world endures, may I also remain to dispel the suffering of the world!

translator_notes: The famous Bodhisattva vow of eternal, selfless service. It is the ultimate statement of resilience, choosing to stay present as an anchor of healing for as long as anyone is in pain.

text_modern: May all the suffering of the world ripen within me, and may the world find true happiness through all the wholesome deeds of the Bodhisattvas!

translator_notes: The practice of Tonglen (taking and sending). A radical psychological willingness to hold the pain of others, offering them our own peace, safety, and joy in return.

text_modern: The sole medicine for the world's pain, the source of all prosperity and happiness—may the path of truth endure for a long, long time, honored and supported by all!

translator_notes: A wish for the preservation of spiritual and psychological truth. Wisdom and compassion are the ultimate medicine for the wounds of the world; may they always be protected.

text_modern: I bow to Mañjughosha, by whose grace my mind is directed toward the good. I honor the holy Spiritual Friend, through whose kindness my heart continues to open!

translator_notes: A final expression of deep gratitude. Healing is only possible through the presence of wise guides (the Spiritual Friend) and our innate capacity for clarity, keeping us humble and connected.
